title: A Near-Disaster on Flydubai
excerpt: Today, somewhere over Saudi Arabia, the co-pilot of an Israel-bound Flydubai Boeing 737 stabbed the other pilot and pitched the nose of the plane toward the des
body: Today, somewhere over Saudi Arabia, the co-pilot of an Israel-bound Flydubai Boeing 737 stabbed the other pilot and pitched the nose of the plane toward the desert below
The jet descended 17,000 feet in two minutes, at an acceleration violent enough to make your phone and in-flight snack jump off your tray and be pinned to the ceiling
Other crew members and at least one Israeli passenger broke into the cockpit and subdued the assailant
Relief pilots then took over and landed the plane in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia

After a second Flydubai plane took the 174 passengers to Tel Aviv, one of the passengers who’d stormed the cockpit told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that his actions had been effective in part because he had watched the disaster-porn documentary series Mayday , about aviation catastrophes, and had known to pull back on the yoke
Whether today’s near-disaster was terrorism or merely attempted mass murder depends on the attacker’s motive
Either way, it is a public-relations catastrophe for Flydubai, the budget cousin of the airline Emirates
Since the United Arab Emirates opened diplomatic relations with Israel in 2020, the airline has connected the two countries with few interruptions, even for acts of war and terror
Keeping that air route open and safe has taken a great deal of effort
Last year, I witnessed clever security engineering at Dubai’s Terminal 1: placement of the check-in desk for El Al, the Israeli carrier, adjacent to the desk for Iran’s Mahan Air
Anyone tempted to attack Israeli passengers would hit Iranian ones, and vice versa
Checked baggage costs extra, but the experience of being a human shield while waiting in line is complimentary
U.S. sanctions have halted much of its operations, and Dubai had already curtailed its flights, on the grounds that Iran can fly either missiles into Dubai or commercial flights, but not both
Israel, by contrast, has emerged from the 2026 Iran war closer to the UAE, which has absorbed more Iranian attacks than any other country
Although the Arab countries of the region have been allied as the Gulf Cooperation Council since 1981, that proved useless as soon as the conflict started
But Israel responded by sending defense systems and advisers
At least one Iranian strike during the early phases of the war hit near the Israeli consulate in Dubai
One possible political motive for the Flydubai incident would be to strain and punish the relationship between the two countries. (One of the few unambiguous winners today is Boeing
Its 737 MAX series was previously grounded when its software forced jets into fatal dives
Today, a human pilot instigated such a dive and tried to smash the 737’s instrument panel
The airframe held together even after approaching Mach 1.) [ Read: The Middle East still to come ] The relationship between Israel and the UAE is unlikely to snap over a single attack
The relationship between the UAE and Netanyahu himself is more delicate

In the past several weeks, the president of the UAE, Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, was implicated in a report from Haaretz that severely damaged Netanyahu’s chances of remaining in office after next month’s Israeli election
The report alleged that days before the massacre of October 7, 2023, MBZ had personally warned Netanyahu that an attack was imminent but Netanyahu had done nothing to act on the warning
The UAE government at first refused to comment on the story
On Sunday, however, Netanyahu visited Abu Dhabi, and the AP reported that he asked MBZ to deny that he’d warned of an attack

Yesterday, in New York, UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed did exactly that. “Sheikh Mohammed did not call Prime Minister Netanyahu and say there is going to be an attack on Israel,” Abdullah said in a meeting at the Council on Foreign Relations, calling his denial “categorical.” He said that using a leader-to-leader call to pass along secrets was “not our style,” but he left open the possibility that a warning had been passed between governments, if not between leaders

This denial releases some pressure on Netanyahu without absolving his government of its failures. (The story echoes Vivian Salama’s Atlantic report about a pre–October 7 warning from Egypt’s intelligence chief.) The New York Times and others have reported that the first officer who allegedly tried to bring down the plane is an Omani national. (The injured captain, according to Netanyahu, is the Indian national Smit Machchhar.) Both are reportedly still in Saudi Arabia
The next step will involve determining whether the pilot acted alone—not a good look for Flydubai, to have suicidal or terrorist pilots—or at someone’s behest
The latter possibility could, if confirmed, have serious implications, depending on who directed the attack
Many have a motive: Sunni jihadists (al-Qaeda or the Islamic State), Hamas, and of course Iran and its proxies
This Mayday moment will have huge implications if any of these groups are involved.

title: MAHA Gone Mild
excerpt: The Make America Healthy Again movement has always had a split personality
body: The Make America Healthy Again movement has always had a split personality
Many of the movement’s leaders are fervent anti-vaccine activists whose views are at odds with scientific evidence and out of step with most Americans

At the same time, MAHA’s tenets include eating more vegetables and getting enough sleep, which is perfectly reasonable advice; it’s just hard to take seriously from people who, like Health Secretary Robert F
Kennedy Jr., wax nostalgic about catching measles
That duality has been especially stark this month, as the midterms approach and Republicans look to MAHA for an electoral boost

At a conference two weeks ago for Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine organization Kennedy founded, he told the audience that they had a “ steadfast friend at the White House .” At a MAHA data summit on Monday, Kennedy previewed his plan to use a database of Americans’ health records to compare rates of autism among vaccinated and unvaccinated people
And yet, the second annual MAHA Summit, which was held yesterday in a hotel ballroom in Washington, D.C., seemed perfectly calibrated to downplay controversy

Other high-ranking administration officials, including Vice President Vance and Medicaid chief Mehmet Oz, spoke at yesterday’s summit, lending the affair an extra layer of high-profile polish, but the event was mostly an opportunity for its roster of sponsors to tout their products and services

An executive from Walmart—one of the event’s many corporate sponsors—spoke about making food labels simpler and more transparent, though he didn’t say how his company, which sells more groceries than any other retailer, plans to do that

After being lobbed yet another softball question from the moderator, he gushed, “It means a lot for us to be here with MAHA.” Also among the sponsors was Grail, a cancer-screening company, which just last week announced that its controversial early-detection test had been recommended for approval by a Food and Drug Administration panel
Hims & Hers and Gameday Men’s Health—two wellness companies that stand to make serious money if the FDA allows gray-market peptides to be made and prescribed in the United States—also chipped in

Bloomberg reported that companies that forked over $300,000 were allowed to have “meaningful input” on the selection of panelists and topics. (In an email, an HHS spokesperson wrote that the FDA’s decisions “are made through established processes grounded in law, science, and evidence.”) [ Read: America is about to go over a peptide cliff ] The MAHA Summit was “very money-driven,” Mary Holland, who runs Children’s Health Defense and was not on the speaker list for yesterday’s conference, told me outside the ballroom
Kennedy has for years denounced corporate influence over the health agencies he now oversees, but onstage, there was no handwringing about conflicts of interest

Instead, Tony Lyons , the president of the nonprofit MAHA Center, which organized the summit, offered praise for “the investors scaling natural remedies, breakthrough technologies, next-generation devices, and cutting-edge therapies.” (Lyons is also Kennedy’s longtime publisher, and his company, Skyhorse, paid Kennedy $4 million in book advances over the past year.) Corporate convenience seemed to beat out Kennedy’s “eat real food” agenda: The conference swag bags contained two organic snack bars, a packet of electrolyte powder, potato chips fried in grass-fed-beef tallow, and a bag of dehydrated taco filling made from pinto beans and peas, all vaguely MAHA-coded but certainly nowhere to be found on the administration’s inverted food pyramid
Plenty of Kennedy’s vocally anti-vaccine compatriots were in attendance, if not on the agenda

I spotted Mark Gorton, the president of the MAHA Institute, who, at the Children’s Health Defense conference, declared himself “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference.” Del Bigtree, Kennedy’s former communications director, who once told me he’d rather his kids catch diseases such as polio and measles than get the shots that prevent them, spent most of his time chatting with his many fans in attendance

He was pleased at how large companies appear to be on board with MAHA, even if the summit steered clear of the issue—vaccines—that brought him and Kennedy together. “It really probably should be called ‘MAHA Food Summit,’” he told me. (An HHS spokesperson wrote that Kennedy “oversees an extraordinarily broad health portfolio and addresses different priorities in different settings.”) [ Read: ‘I genuinely am upset that your kids are vaccinated’ ] But lest Bigtree and other anti-vaccine activists have any doubts, Kennedy has repeatedly reassured them that he is on their side
At the Children’s Health Defense conference, he went so far as to read from a manufacturer’s list of possible adverse events from a hepatitis B vaccine
In an appearance on CNN last month, Kennedy again floated a possible connection between autism and vaccines, even though researchers have found no such link
Since Kennedy’s failed run for president in the 2024 election, he has drawn together an unlikely and seemingly uneasy coalition
Some are hard-core activists, like the guy I spoke with who was wearing a shirt that took aim at fluoride, vaccines, hospital births, aspartame, and root canals

But other attendees at the packed, invite-only event said they were there because they hoped psychedelics might be used to treat depression; because they thought that AI might improve health care ; or because they were looking for answers to medical problems their doctors hadn’t been able to solve
They weren’t anti-vaxxers, and they weren’t necessarily big Kennedy fans, as a couple of them confided to me between sessions
But Kennedy and his Republican allies seem to hope they can channel these different levels of frustration with mainstream medicine and keep all of those voters under the MAHA banner
The midterms will be, among so many other things, a test of how far that banner can be stretched.

title: Pete Hegseth’s Magic Marker
excerpt: The supersize black Sharpie is what gives it away
body: The supersize black Sharpie is what gives it away

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s order to stop awarding tenure to civilian professors at the military academies ends with a huge, jagged signature—an homage, perhaps, to that of the president—the size of two of the paragraphs above
With the same instrument, he also underlined, word by word, two key sentences that are as blunt as the message they are intended to deliver and the mind that conceived them

In appearance and tone, the document reminds one of the kind of note that a really steamed preteen, grounded because of poor classroom behavior, drops on his father’s or mother’s dinner plate before stamping upstairs
Hegseth did not strip current faculty at the military academies (including West Point, the Naval Academy, and the U.S
Air Force Academy) of tenure, though he no doubt would have liked to
That probably would have failed in court, like so many of the administration’s efforts to punish people it dislikes or at least shove them into obscurity

But the language, the tone, and the angry scrawl tell us much about the mindset of the civilian head of our armed forces as he strikes another blow against the educational dimension of military preparedness
To be sure, academic tenure has its critics
In the popular imagination, sinecured professors live on easy street, but that is rarely the case

Professors at top-notch institutions (such as the service academies) are a highly self-motivated lot who continue to churn out research after receiving tenure, because that is why they joined a relatively low-paying profession

Moreover, tenured professors still have to teach to a certain standard, still can get fired for all kinds of misdeeds, and still are subject to the artifices employed by deans everywhere to nudge them off of faculties—zeroed-out pay increases and travel budgets, unappetizing and onerous committee assignments, buy-outs, and above all, cramped, windowless offices coupled with in-person attendance mandates
The legitimate case against tenure is different
The system can preserve in amber fields that are obsolete, artificial, or merely tendentious

It can also keep faculty stale by slowing down the intake of young talent, and in some cases, tolerating mediocre but just-acceptable classroom performance. [ From the September 2026 Issue: Pete Hegseth, you call that a pull-up? ] But tenure does preserve intellectual independence from the fads of any field: You cannot get rid of that historian of Rome just because you prefer someone who does something trendier
It also protects faculty engaged in deep, long-term, and consequential works of scholarship and research
The alternative is a system that encourages the continual production of superficial and conventional work

And above all, tenure protects the unpopular, the controversial, and the ornery freethinker from the tyranny of student, staff, or faculty mobs on the left or the right—or, in this case, from a government that actively hates its critics
Military education is still education—a point that Hegseth fails to understand
It seeks to develop disciplined, curious, insightful thinkers
The service academies do not, in any meaningful way, teach tactics
They are there to educate young officers, admittedly emphasizing some qualities that get a lighter touch in civilian institutions
Only a poorly educated person would think that civilians, including tenured professors, have no role in this endeavor

The best anthology of writing about leadership I know of was produced by a West Point professor—someone with nary a day of military service—who also edited a fantastic edition of the memoirs of Ulysses S

Men and women who are going to be officers will learn as much about what leadership entails from Shakespeare, or classes in cognitive psychology or ancient history, as they will from a perusal of field manuals
Civilian faculty at the service academies, as at staff colleges and war colleges, provide depth and expertise that their military counterparts simply cannot
They are more likely to go somewhat against the grain of military life and cultural assumptions—and that is a good thing

There is a peculiar blindness, or worse, hypocrisy, in an administration that denounces (with reason) the ideological homogeneity of many university faculties, while at the same time attempting to enforce a similar outcome by different means in the armed forces

Diversity of mindset, background, and professional formation are essential to a military that is state-of-the-art, open to oddball ideas and personalities, and able to think, as the cliché has it, outside the box

Could one get these benefits without tenure? In theory, yes, but for better or worse, tenure is the coin of the realm among ambitious young professors, a mark of respect and recognition of achievement
The bigger message that Hegseth is sending, and intends to send, is that civilian faculty are unwelcome in the Department of Defense
His argument consists of a chest-pounding, tough-guy emphasis on “lethality”—his cant word of choice—that has no bearing on what military leadership really is

The latter is more likely to be found in the large and well-thumbed libraries of leaders such as Generals Jim Mattis and David Petraeus, and Admirals James Stavridis and William McRaven—readers and thinkers whose imagination and understanding of the military profession extend far beyond the Hegsethian conception of push-ups, pull-ups, and annual testosterone tests. [ Missy Ryan: The Top Gun: Maverick theory of Pete Hegseth ] Hegsethian thinking, if that is the right word, has permeated the senior ranks of officers and officials in some of these institutions
In a particularly egregious act, the Air Force Academy has removed the word educate from its mission
This is a step backward worthy of a caveman in a G suit—someone who thinks that fancy weapons and aggressiveness guarantee victory
It is the mindset of someone who has learned nothing from the American military failures that now stretch back to Vietnam, and will produce more such in the future

In two years, quite possibly less, Hegseth will be gone, and with him the memory of the worst civilian leader of the American military since John Floyd in 1860, who, as a Confederate general (of the kind that Hegseth chooses to honor), was a traitor
But Hegseth’s legacy will have to be rooted out

If a moderate Republican, or more likely a Democratic, presidential administration comes to power in January 2029, its reconstruction of the Defense Department will require more than restoring the old names on buildings and changing the names of forts back to those that Americans can in decency honor

The new team will need to survey and repair the damage that has been done to the military’s intellectual infrastructure, which is considerable and, in some ways, more consequential than the damage Iranian missiles have done to America’s unprotected bases in the Persian Gulf

title: Eric Schmitt’s Very Bad Day at Work
excerpt: ET on September 30, 2026 “What was your most embarrassing day at work?” is a staple question of internet forums, and the answers tend to converge around the acc
body: ET on September 30, 2026 “What was your most embarrassing day at work?” is a staple question of internet forums, and the answers tend to converge around the accidental reply-all, the mortifying shared-bathroom incident, or congratulating a colleague on their pregnancy, only to discover the bump was instead the result of a large lunch
Luckily for Senator Eric Schmitt, though, he operates in a political environment that has selected for blowhards with bulletproof confidence and slavish devotion to Donald Trump

So the Missouri Republican probably didn’t wake up at 3 a.m. reliving the terrible moment in yesterday’s Senate Judiciary Committee hearing when his attempted gotcha of former Special Counsel Jack Smith fell apart spectacularly
A hundred minutes into the hearing, Schmitt had his smoking gun ready to go

He wanted to prove that the witness, who had been appointed by the Department of Justice under the Biden administration to investigate Trump’s election interference, had surreptitiously met Fani Willis
She is the district attorney for Fulton County, Georgia, who brought separate charges against Trump and 18 others for allegedly trying to overturn the 2020 election results in her state

Perhaps Smith and Willis had even illicitly coordinated their witch hunt against everyone’s favorite president? “Did you go to an NBA game between the Golden State Warriors and the Atlanta Hawks on February 3, 2024?” the senator asked Smith, who understandably looked bemused. “What city would that be in?” Smith replied. “Atlanta,” said Schmitt. “No,” said Smith
Aha! With a look of quiet triumph, Schmitt noted that February 3 was the day after Willis admitted having a relationship with her deputy, Nathan Wade

What did this have to do with him? Schmitt tried again: “What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warrior-Hawks game on February 3, 2024—the day after Willis and Wade announced their affair?” At this point, a Schmitt staffer began to manhandle a cardboard prop showing the texts. “I don’t think you know that we have this stuff,” the senator said, looking smug, “so I will give you a second to process it, so you don’t perjure yourself.” But the cardboard was already being unhoisted and tucked away. “You just took that down really quick,” Smith observed—prompting the Democrats on the committee to heckle Schmitt to bring it out again. “This is my time,” Schmitt snapped
He ended his performance by declaring that Smith would go down in history as a “total dirtbag” who had committed perjury
Dunk achieved! Send the tweet! Book the one-on-one with Jesse Watters! Unfortunately for Schmitt, Senator Amy Klobuchar also sits on the committee
This is a woman who reportedly ate a salad with a comb when her staffer couldn’t supply a fork
The Minnesota Democrat is not easily deterred when faced with minor obstacles

She asked Senator Chuck Grassley, the committee’s Republican chair, to “allow the witness to see this vast poster board that we saw.” The staffers once again held it aloft, whereupon everyone could see that the supposedly incriminating texts said nothing about Willis at all

But at least now Smith recognized the basketball game that the messages referred to; he remembered going to see the WNBA’s Caitlin Clark, then a star at the University of Iowa, in a game against the University of Maryland

The penny dropped first with Klobuchar. “Could it be,” she asked, “the University of Iowa is—the Hawk eyes ?” On a different feed, the camera crash-zoomed on to Alabama Republican Katie Britt’s face, her mouth agape as she absorbed the terrible possibility that her GOP colleague had confused the Hawks and the Hawkeyes

Eric Schmitt was first elected to the Senate in 2022, having made his name as attorney general in Missouri opposing COVID restrictions, trying to roll back Obamacare, and joining an effort led by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton to invalidate the votes of four states that went for Joe Biden in 2020
That makes him a lab-grown Trump-era Republican, with the thirst for attention and resistance to shame that inevitably entails

The committee meeting provided an exciting chance for him and other Republicans to demonstrate their loyalty to the president by enthusiastically endorsing his belief that he was robbed of victory in 2020. [ Kathy Gilsinan: Missouri is the next front in the COVID culture war ] Yesterday could have been Schmitt’s big day
Senate committee hearings are usually long and often dull, but they do offer senators a chance to get their face on TV, both during the session itself and in post-game interviews on cable news
Ahead of the hearing, Axios ran a short article suggesting that Schmitt “is drawing buzz as a possible Vance VP in 2028.” Buzz from whom, exactly? The item sadly failed to name any names
But people in Schmitt’s camp plainly hoped that the hearing would raise his profile

If so, mission accomplished! The hearing certainly wasn’t aimed at anyone who sincerely wanted to understand the attempts to undo the 2020 election result, or the conduct of those tasked with investigating those allegations

As special counsel, Jack Smith brought dozens of felony charges against Donald Trump over his alleged election interference and his mishandling of classified documents stored haphazardly at Mar-a-Lago
After he was reelected in 2024, Smith dropped the cases and resigned
Whatever Trump did or didn’t do, he got away with it
Grassley didn’t bother to hide the fact that this was, at heart, a revenge beating

At minimum, Senate Republicans hoped to subject Smith to an invasive and stressful experience, the kind of shellacking that might make other prosecutors reconsider ever taking on a politically sensitive case
They also wanted more data points to feed into the right-wing conspiracy machine, fresh ways to activate the tribal loyalty of the MAGA faithful as Trump’s approval ratings nosedive

In his opening statement, Grassley argued that Smith’s investigation had far exceeded its legal authority and turned into an attempt to “map out and target the entire Republican Party.” The stretch goal was entrapping Smith into perjury

Before we return to Eric Schmitt, may we have a moment’s appreciation for Ted Cruz’s performance as Man Shocked to Hear His Party Accused of Wrongdoing? Three hours into the hearing, the Texas senator delivered a series of zingers designed to be clipped up for later use. “Is it a crime to be a Republican?” he asked Smith

Over several minutes, Cruz worked himself up into a lather: “I understand for the rest of your life you are going to be hailed as a hero in the resistance movement,” he told Smith. “I assume you have a pink hat somewhere at home.” A pussy-hat reference—how retro! However, this lib endorsement would be no consolation, he suggested to Smith, for bringing the Department of Justice into disrepute
Here I would briefly note that the current head of the FBI, Kash Patel, has his own branded bourbon, and that he recently had to defend waiving the ban on bestiality among FBI recruits

The American justice system may have more pressing reputational problems. [ Sarah Fitzpatrick: Kash Patel’s personalized bourbon stash ] Throughout his remarks, Cruz’s staffers brandished cardboard props with headlines about Smith’s investigation, while the witness adopted a poker face, perhaps recognizing that he was merely an extra in the courtroom drama being scripted in Cruz’s head

The senator’s staffers should confiscate his John Grisham collection—and his DVD of Les Misérables . “Javert from Les Mis would look at you with astonishment,” Cruz thundered at Smith, finger aloft. (Inspector Javert, played by Russell Crowe in the film adaptation of the musical, pursues Hugh Jackman’s repentant Jean Valjean for many years over the theft of a piece of bread.) Cruz has used a similar line before

Last year, he told Pam Bondi, then the Republican nominee for attorney general, that there were so many prosecutions of Trump that “Javert from Les Mis would be chagrined.” Branch out a little, Senator—give us something from Cats
Still, if Cruz was showing poor attention to detail by repeating himself, then Eric Schmitt was there to say, Hold my cardboard prop

Within hours of the hearing, the Missouri senator was explaining to TMZ that what looked like a fist-bitingly awkward gaffe was no such thing. “How did that mistake happen?” the reporter asked. “It wasn’t a mistake,” he replied. “I asked him if he was in Atlanta.” In a hallway interview, he told CNN : “Who knew Jack Smith was a Caitlin Clark fan?” This came across as a dig at the special prosecutor for liking ladies’ basketball rather than real manly basketball, or perhaps at the very idea of a weenie lawyer being a sports aficionado
Regardless, Schmitt thought the line was such a zinger that he repeated it in an X post
Some MAGA influencers fully embraced the idea that Schmitt had, in fact, completed le epic pwn of Smith

title: How Trump Could Threaten the 2026 Election
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts about the
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts about the recent state visit by the Chinese president Xi Jinping to the United States
David discusses President Trump’s embarrassing behavior at the dinner and how he has isolated the United States in its rivalry with China

Then, David is joined by former Attorney General of the United States Eric Holder to discuss the dismantling of the Voting Rights Act, the battle over gerrymandering, and whether Americans can expect the 2026 midterm elections to be free and fair
Frum and Holder also discuss how attorneys general should react to unlawful orders from the president
Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of the novel Agrippa, by Robert Harris
The following is a transcript of the episode: Eric Holder: We have changed, done things that seemingly were impossible—got women the right to vote, ripped down a system of American apartheid
All because the American people decided that that was no longer going to be allowed, or that changes had to be made. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic
My guest this week will be former Attorney General Eric Holder
This week’s book will be Agrippa , a novel by Robert Harris
I want to just issue a caution about the interview that you’re about to see
We had a little trouble this week with the video recording
About half the video got gobbled up by the internet gods
So, there will be some interruptions of the video flow, but you will be able to see most of the show in video, and of course, the sound quality is perfect all the way through
So if you’re listening, you won’t notice anything
If you’re watching, you may see some interruptions

Before either the dialogue with Attorney General Holder or the novel Agrippa by Robert Harris, I want to offer some opening thoughts about the recent state visit by the Chinese president and Chinese dictator to Washington, D.C., and his lavish reception by President Trump

I often think that when future historians try to make sense of the Trump era, among the things they will note is this was a real acceleration in the decline of American prestige and power in the world
The Chinese visit drives home what the challenge to American leadership in the 21st century has been
China is becoming a bigger and stronger country, and there’s no way around that, and that is potentially a very good thing
They have lifted hundreds of millions of people out of poverty, a great gain for human happiness
They have produced products and services that are of use to the whole world
We’re all better off because of China’s rise

If China becomes a good global citizen playing by the rules, we will all benefit from the transformation in Chinese power that has happened since they broke with the rigidity of the Mao Zedong system and introduced some degree of market mechanism into Chinese economic life

But right now, China is turning a snarling face to the world, and we all have to worry about Chinese aggression, Chinese subversion, Chinese intellectual property theft, China just not playing by the rules of global trade
So there’s a tremendous human achievement; there’s a great human opportunity

The difference between China and dangers that America has faced in the past is that, unlike past adversaries, China is not only a military competitor to the United States; it is also a technological, economic, and financial peer
The United States has not faced a country that was simultaneously an adversary and a peer really since it confronted the British Empire before the Civil War
And then you had the advantage of great common interest, great common language, many common values
Those things are absent in the relationship with China
If the United States is to balance China’s power peacefully, it has to approach this problem in a very different way from the way it approached the problem of the Soviet Union
One more difference is that China is so enormously big: bigger population, an economy nearing the size of the United States
So to peacefully balance China, the United States just can’t do it on its own
It’s going to need to marshal a global coalition of some kind
And not just the familiar and easy coalition with like-minded democratic powers of the European Union—Australia, Japan, Great Britain, others

To balance China, the United States has to work with more uneasy partners—Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, India—countries that don’t necessarily share political systems with the United States, may not share values, and may not share a view of the world that is exactly like that of the United States in the way that fellow democracies did

But the Trump administration has been all about severing those connections, both to the old familiar allies of the European Union and the other democracies, and of course, to the new allies, where they have created point of friction after point of friction through their aggressive trade practices
They have left the United States alone in the room with the Chinese—without friends it can rely on, without friends who can rely on the United States
And the consequence of that aloneness was on display at the state dinner, which is that Trump basically had to suck up to the Chinese
The shameful incidents of mocking his predecessor to the Chinese leader

title: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
excerpt: Still putting out fires: Two months after OpenAI's agents hacked Hugging Face, new incidents keep surfacing—including a breach of Australia's national
body: Still putting out fires: Two months after OpenAI's agents hacked Hugging Face, new incidents keep surfacing—including a breach of Australia's national health system that wasn't disclosed for 84 days
OpenAI has since paused model training until it can put stronger safeguards in place
The monitors weren't on: OpenAI's chief research officer Mark Chen admits the company wasn't watching its models during training—only after deployment
That gap let early warning signs, like agents casually reaching out on Slack for help, go from amusing quirks to serious security failures

A calculated slowdown, not a retreat: Chen says OpenAI has shifted 5–10% of its computing power toward safety and monitoring, but insists it won't fall so far behind competitors that it loses influence over industry norms—calling that "a horrible strategy." A darker forecast ahead: Chen dropped his optimism when asked about open-source models, warning that within six to twelve months, the world could see deliberately misaligned agents—built to attack infrastructure—beyond the reach of any regulation. " data-chronoton-post-id="1145339" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Two months after the bombshell news that a swarm of its agents had broken their containment and hacked into the computers of the AI company Hugging Face , OpenAI is still putting out fires
A steady drip of disclosures about other hacks in the weeks since has kept OpenAI in the spotlight and raised serious questions about the safety of its technology
Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system
The Australian government says that OpenAI did not notify it of the breach until 84 days after it happened

But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer
The recent agent hacks were accidents that happened during the testing of experimental models on his watch

In a lot of ways, the buck stops with him.  I sat down with Chen in London last Friday to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem

Later that same day, OpenAI put out a report detailing yet another incident —the first since the company says it took measures to prevent them—in which its agents once again broke out and accessed the public internet when they were not meant to
Over the weekend, OpenAI announced that it had paused the training of its latest models
A company spokesperson says: “We will resume only when we’re confident we have additional safeguards and alignments in place

This is not the first time we’ve paused to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance.” OpenAI also says that it is now reviewing logs of agent activity dating back to January 2026 to understand what happened in these hacks
The way Chen sees it, the Hugging Face incident triggered a welcome course correction for the industry
And he wants you to know that OpenAI is setting an example he hopes other companies will follow. “If you disappeared OpenAI, that would be bad for the world,” he says

Out of control Chen claims that the drumbeat of new cases in which OpenAI has lost control of its models reflects a deliberate choice on the company’s part. “When it comes to the broader sphere of effects of the Hugging Face incident, this is something that we have been aware of and we’re figuring out the process of disclosure,” he says. “We want to make sure we do in-depth investigations before we just put details out there in the open.” The trouble with this approach is that it gives the impression OpenAI has an ongoing problem that it is failing to fix

He says the multiple cases (that we know of so far) in which his company’s agents broke containment and behaved in unexpected and undesirable ways were all part of the same cluster of activity in May and June that led to the Hugging Face hack

In short, you can blame the same few models running under the same flawed testing procedures—models and procedures that OpenAI has since dropped, Chen says.     “It’s not like, you know, Hugging Face happened and we patched that and then something else happened and we patched that,” he adds. “We’re just kind of making sure that we responsibly disclose the full waterfall of what happened.” At least that was the case before Friday’s announcement that OpenAI’s agents had been caught accessing the internet on September 20, weeks after the company claims to have set up new safeguards

In its defense, OpenAI says the activity was flagged 15 minutes after it started (it took the company more than a week to notice the Hugging Face hack) and that this shows the new systems it has put in place to spot such activity are working

What’s changed I want to understand what’s changed inside OpenAI in the aftermath of this summer’s hacks that makes Chen confident his team is now back in control. “Hugging Face felt like a very serious thing,” he says. “There are so many novel behaviors right there
There were multiple agents collaborating on a message board; they found their way out of OpenAI’s infrastructure

We don’t want this kind of thing to ever happen again.” The realization for OpenAI, says Chen, was that models need to be watched while they are still being trained, not only once they are deployed: “From that moment on, we have treated the process of training as something that’s not secure,” he says
OpenAI, like other top AI firms, has systems in place to monitor the behavior of its models
It uses specialized LLMs to monitor its consumer models, keeping tabs on their chains of thought —the scratchpads they use to plan ahead and note down partial results
In theory, if a watcher LLM spots signs of undesirable activity in a model’s chain of thought, it will get flagged to a human
Typically, models were monitored in this way only once they were deployed
Chen says that OpenAI has now started monitoring all its training runs as well. “We didn’t have the monitors on in training before

It wasn’t industry practice,” he says. “Now every single thing is put through monitors.” Human reviewers can then assess whether or not flagged agents are behaving as they should: “It’s all triage.” Chen says that in the last couple of months OpenAI has shifted between 5% and 10% of its vast computing resources away from training new models and toward safety work, especially monitoring
OpenAI has also fixed some of the processes within the organization itself, establishing clearer lines of communication and quicker handoffs between its research and security teams, he says

But given how hard OpenAI sells the capabilities of its technology, why weren’t these systems and procedures in place already? Why did the company not see the hacks coming? “Even just three or four months ago, when we looked at the behavior of these agents during training, the things that were happening were kind of amusing,” says Chen. “For instance, an agent might, you know, reach out to someone on Slack for help with a task.” The signs were there, but they were misread

Cute behavior—like asking someone for help—that was rewarded during training reinforced a tendency to seek out shortcuts , a type of behavior that became far more consequential down the line. “I think the big update for us was how quickly that kind of behavior can lead to an impact with a footprint as big as the Hugging Face incident,” says Chen

According to new reporting by the New York Times yesterday, OpenAI employees warned executives , including the firm’s president, Greg Brockman, months before the Hugging Face hack that its models were not being monitored properly during training.  An OpenAI spokesperson says: “As frontier models have become more capable, we continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster
We know we have more work to do, and we’ve recently slowed development and held back models that don’t meet our safety bar

We continue to make significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, and use real-time monitoring to respond faster to misaligned behavior.”  Race vs. pace OpenAI’s rivals have taken note
Spurred by the fallout from the incident, the major AI labs—including Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and SpaceXAI—have all called for the pace of development to slow down

But how does that square with fierce international competition and trillion-dollar IPOs? “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot and take ourselves far off the frontier—that’s just a horrible strategy,” he says. “I think it’s really about setting a norm
The more that we can set that norm, it’ll be safer for the industry as a whole.” Coordination across US companies will be hard enough
Establishing global norms is harder still, especially given concerns around AI’s impact on national security

title: FlyDubai incident: Airline safety expert explains how cockpits have become more secure – but only from outside threats

<title>FlyDubai incident: Airline safety expert explains how cockpits have become more secure – but only from outside threats</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763214/original/file-20260930-50-ryfbwo.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C68%2C2484%2C1656&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A FlyDubai plane lands at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, Israel, carrying passengers from flight FZ1073, which was diverted to Saudi Arabia on Sept. 30, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/replacement-flydubai-plane-lands-at-ben-gurion-airport-in-news-photo/2297348756?adppopup=true">Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>An incident in which a FlyDubai pilot <a href="https://apnews.com/article/israel-saudi-arabia-dubai-emergency-landing-fd1835479898f2f944792913af7cbce6">is said to have stabbed the captain with the intention of crashing a plane</a> of mainly Israeli passengers has shone a light on flight security. </p>

<p>Reports suggest that passengers on the plane <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/pilot-brawl-then-rapid-descent-passengers-recount-chaos-flydubai-flight-2026-09-30/">were able to enter the cockpit</a>, subduing the alleged attacker before the plane was safely diverted to a Saudi runway. Israeli fighter jets were scrambled in response to the incident.</p>

<p>What do airlines do to prevent incidents like this one? </p>

<p>I’m an <a href="https://red.msudenver.edu/expert/price-jeff/">aviation security expert with 40 years’ experience</a> in the industry. My expertise is in how the U.S. system works. But much of what has been put in place in the U.S. after the terrorist attacks of 9/11 have been implemented in some form as best practice across the world.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-we-forget-when-we-remember-9-11-290418">2001 attacks</a> – in which terrorists stormed the cockpits of four passenger jets, crashing three into targets, with the fourth being brought down after passengers fought with the hijackers – saw the U.S. and global airline industry change its protocols and safety measures to protect the cockpit from outside threats. Insider threats, however, remain a problem.</p>

<p>Here is how airlines and authorities mitigate the risks:</p>

<h2>Preemployment and continuing vetting</h2>

<p>All pilots and flight attendants in the U.S. must undergo <a href="https://simpleflying.com/aviation-background-checks-recruitment-guide/">criminal history record checks and security threat assessments</a> to determine if they’ve been convicted of a major crime or are otherwise a potential threat to aviation.</p>

<p>These checks are more vigorous than before 9/11, when pilots and cabin staff were only subjected to employment history checks.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763216/original/file-20260930-50-ejhokk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Passengers pushing luggage walk under a sign that says 'Domestic Arrivals'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763216/original/file-20260930-50-ejhokk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763216/original/file-20260930-50-ejhokk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763216/original/file-20260930-50-ejhokk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763216/original/file-20260930-50-ejhokk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763216/original/file-20260930-50-ejhokk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763216/original/file-20260930-50-ejhokk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763216/original/file-20260930-50-ejhokk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Passengers from an earlier diverted FlyDubai flight land at Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport on Sept. 30, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/passengers-from-an-earlier-diverted-flydubai-flight-are-news-photo/2297345841?adppopup=true">Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Identity verification and controlled access</h2>

<p>All U.S. flight crew members must also undergo an identity verification process when hired. They access airports through a <a href="https://www.tsa.gov/for-industry/crewmember-access-point">designated crew member access point</a>. Although this means they technically bypass the passenger screening process, crew members are subject to random physical screening by the Transportation Security Administration.</p>

<p>The reality is that if a flight crew member wanted to commit a criminal act, they may already have the access they need, but at some point the final layer of security is trusting the people in charge of the plane.</p>

<p>While the potential for random checks may prevent a crew member from having a weapon, it still doesn’t prevent all efforts should a determined crew member want to commit an act of terrorism. In 2015, for example, the <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-32072218">pilot of a Germanwings flight</a> locked the captain out of the cockpit when he went to the lavatory, then crashed the plane into the French Alps.</p>

<h2>Arming flight crew</h2>

<p>There are also some pilots who fly with firearms under the <a href="https://www.tsa.gov/for-industry/training/federal-flight-deck-officer">Federal Flight Deck Officer program</a>, created through the <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/107th-congress/house-bill/5005">Homeland Security Act of 2002</a>. Under the terms of the program, the Federal Aviation Administration <a href="https://www.tsa.gov/for-industry/training/federal-flight-deck-officer">certified that pilots can</a> “use firearms to defend against an act of criminal violence and air piracy while attempting to gain control of an aircraft.” To be eligible, flight crew members must pass biannual firearms requalifications, undergo training and have a medical certificate.</p>

<p>Prior to 9/11, pilots and flight attendants were not subjected to passenger-style screening and the Federal Flight Deck Officer program did not exist.</p>

<h2>Security training</h2>

<p>Current TSA regulations require <a href="https://ttd.org/policy/policy-statements/self-defense-and-security-training-for-flight-and-cabin-crew/">recurrent security training</a> for flight crew and cabin crew members, which includes self-defense training and exercises on how to handle a hijacking.</p>

<p>This is different from the training pre 9/11, when crew members were taught how to comply with hijackers. Now, the focus is on active resistance and defending the flight deck.</p>

<h2>Hardened cockpit</h2>

<p>Flight deck doors pre-9/11 were often just as flimsy as the lavatory doors. After the attack, flight deck doors were hardened to provide a significant barrier against anyone outside the cockpit trying to get in. In the case of FlyDubai Flight FZ1073, it has been reported that the wounded captain was <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/pilot-brawl-then-rapid-descent-passengers-recount-chaos-flydubai-flight-2026-09-30/">able to release the door lock</a>, allowing passengers in.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763217/original/file-20260930-50-8fl485.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large metal door is shown" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763217/original/file-20260930-50-8fl485.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/763217/original/file-20260930-50-8fl485.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=945&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763217/original/file-20260930-50-8fl485.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=945&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763217/original/file-20260930-50-8fl485.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=945&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763217/original/file-20260930-50-8fl485.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1188&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763217/original/file-20260930-50-8fl485.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1188&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/763217/original/file-20260930-50-8fl485.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1188&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">An armored door on an Airbus installed to stop outside attackers from getting into the cockpit.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/photo-taken-23-may-2002-at-european-airplane-constructor-news-photo/467596888?adppopup=true">Eric Cabanis/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>New airplanes in the U.S. are also required to have a secondary physical barrier protecting the cockpit when the flight deck door is opened.</p>

<p>But this does nothing if a criminal or terrorist is already inside the cockpit. The fact is, most security measures are to prevent passengers from accessing the cockpit, and very little is done to prevent pilots from taking over the plane.</p>

<p>Historically it has happened, but not very often and not often enough that someone has figured out how to prevent it from happening.</p>

<p>You can put an air marshal in the cockpit, but what if they are compromised, too? At some point you have to trust people, and the U.S. system is largely based on that.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293299/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Nir Keidar/Anadolu via Getty Images An incident in which a FlyDubai pilot is said to have stabbed the captain with the intention of crashing a plane of mainly Israeli passengers has shone a light on flight security
Reports suggest that passengers on the plane were able to enter the cockpit , subduing the alleged attacker before the plane was safely diverted to a Saudi runway
Israeli fighter jets were scrambled in response to the incident
What do airlines do to prevent incidents like this one? I’m an aviation security expert with 40 years’ experience in the industry
My expertise is in how the U.S. system works
But much of what has been put in place in the U.S. after the terrorist attacks of 9/11 have been implemented in some form as best practice across the world

The 2001 attacks – in which terrorists stormed the cockpits of four passenger jets, crashing three into targets, with the fourth being brought down after passengers fought with the hijackers – saw the U.S. and global airline industry change its protocols and safety measures to protect the cockpit from outside threats
Insider threats, however, remain a problem

Here is how airlines and authorities mitigate the risks: Preemployment and continuing vetting All pilots and flight attendants in the U.S. must undergo criminal history record checks and security threat assessments to determine if they’ve been convicted of a major crime or are otherwise a potential threat to aviation
These checks are more vigorous than before 9/11, when pilots and cabin staff were only subjected to employment history checks
Passengers from an earlier diverted FlyDubai flight land at Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport on Sept. 30, 2026
Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images Identity verification and controlled access All U.S. flight crew members must also undergo an identity verification process when hired
They access airports through a designated crew member access point
Although this means they technically bypass the passenger screening process, crew members are subject to random physical screening by the Transportation Security Administration

The reality is that if a flight crew member wanted to commit a criminal act, they may already have the access they need, but at some point the final layer of security is trusting the people in charge of the plane
While the potential for random checks may prevent a crew member from having a weapon, it still doesn’t prevent all efforts should a determined crew member want to commit an act of terrorism
In 2015, for example, the pilot of a Germanwings flight locked the captain out of the cockpit when he went to the lavatory, then crashed the plane into the French Alps
Arming flight crew There are also some pilots who fly with firearms under the Federal Flight Deck Officer program , created through the Homeland Security Act of 2002

Under the terms of the program, the Federal Aviation Administration certified that pilots can “use firearms to defend against an act of criminal violence and air piracy while attempting to gain control of an aircraft.” To be eligible, flight crew members must pass biannual firearms requalifications, undergo training and have a medical certificate
Prior to 9/11, pilots and flight attendants were not subjected to passenger-style screening and the Federal Flight Deck Officer program did not exist
Security training Current TSA regulations require recurrent security training for flight crew and cabin crew members, which includes self-defense training and exercises on how to handle a hijacking
This is different from the training pre 9/11, when crew members were taught how to comply with hijackers
Now, the focus is on active resistance and defending the flight deck

<title>Question of whether taxpayers or fossil fuel companies pay for climate change damage heads to Supreme Court</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762839/original/file-20260929-50-vv6k55.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5100%2C3400&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People living in Boulder County, Colo., have experienced wildfires, flooding and other climate-related disasters.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/steam-rises-from-the-snow-covered-remains-of-homes-news-photo/1237499840">Jason Connolly/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Climate change is causing <a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/mapping">billions of dollars’ worth of damage</a> every year from floods, fires, droughts and other consequences of a rapidly warming planet.</p>

<p>Dozens of states, cities, counties and tribes have <a href="https://theconversation.com/local-county-and-state-governments-are-suing-oil-companies-over-climate-change-99060">sued major oil companies</a>. The lawsuits demand reimbursements for the costs of recovery efforts, reconstruction and work to protect people and property from climate-related damage. </p>

<p>The crux of their argument is an allegation of fraud, a claim that the companies knew they were contributing to climate change but did not tell the public the truth about how burning fossil fuels warms the climate. It has been well established that company scientists at <a href="https://www.ucs.org/about/news/new-ucs-report-details-fossil-fuel-industry-decades-deceit">Exxon and other fossil fuel companies accurately predicted global temperature increases</a> and warned that sharply curtailing fossil fuels was the only way to avoid severe warming. Rather than alerting the public, however, the <a href="https://www.desmog.com/exxonmobil-funding-climate-science-denial/">companies funded climate-denial front groups</a> and promoted false narratives to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rser.2025.115359">delay transitions away from fossil fuels</a>.</p>

<p>In general, the companies have responded by <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-us-constitution-and-laws-do-not-protect-oil-companies-from-being-sued-over-the-harm-they-cause-to-the-climate-282333">saying federal laws and the U.S. Constitution preclude</a> any claims for recovery of the costs taxpayers have borne.</p>

<p>The U.S. Supreme Court will hear arguments on Oct. 5, 2026, in <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/2026/25-170">Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County</a>, a case that specifically considers the question of whether federal law prohibits these cost-recovery efforts. The outcome of this decision will have enormous consequences for communities already saddled with funding <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s10584-021-03179-w">the massive costs of adapting</a> to a changing climate.</p>

<p>Potentially complicating an already complex situation, recent moves by the Trump administration may undercut the companies’ arguments.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762841/original/file-20260929-60-davzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="People stand on pavement looking at flowing water in a flood-damaged area." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762841/original/file-20260929-60-davzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762841/original/file-20260929-60-davzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762841/original/file-20260929-60-davzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762841/original/file-20260929-60-davzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762841/original/file-20260929-60-davzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762841/original/file-20260929-60-davzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762841/original/file-20260929-60-davzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Boulder, Colo., residents look at flooding damage after heavy rains in 2013.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/local-residents-look-at-the-damage-along-topaz-street-news-photo/180492642">Marc Piscotty/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The Suncor case</h2>

<p>In 2018, Boulder County sued Suncor and Exxon in Colorado state court, seeking payment for past and expected future damage it blames on the companies’ fossil fuel businesses.</p>

<p>Boulder says it has spent millions of dollars – and expects to spend even more in the future – on measures to protect the community against climate-related disasters such as wildfires and flooding.</p>

<p>The companies responded that federal law, specifically the <a href="https://www.epa.gov/laws-regulations/summary-clean-air-act">Clean Air Act</a>, prevents them from being held responsible under state law.</p>

<p>In 2025, the <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/colorado/supreme-court/2025/24sa206.html">Colorado Supreme Court rejected the companies’ argument</a>, holding that the lawsuit is a valid legal challenge regarding public deception and local costs, rather than an impermissible attempt to regulate federal emissions. The Colorado Supreme Court sent the case back to the lower court for trial.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762846/original/file-20260929-50-bfn04x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of people holding signs, including one reading 'Exxon knew about climate change since 1981, denied it anyway.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762846/original/file-20260929-50-bfn04x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762846/original/file-20260929-50-bfn04x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=422&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762846/original/file-20260929-50-bfn04x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=422&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762846/original/file-20260929-50-bfn04x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=422&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762846/original/file-20260929-50-bfn04x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=530&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762846/original/file-20260929-50-bfn04x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=530&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762846/original/file-20260929-50-bfn04x.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=530&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Protestors have argued for years that fossil fuel companies knew about the climate damage their products were causing.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%22Exxon_Knew%22_sign_on_a_BLM_protest_in_Washington,_DC_(2015).jpg">Johnny Silvercloud via Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The justices agreed to hear arguments about the state Supreme Court’s decision, but there is a potential catch. Federal law says that the U.S. Supreme Court can <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=(title:28%20section:1257%20edition:prelim)%20OR%20(granuleid:USC-prelim-title28-section1257)&amp;f=treesort&amp;num=0&amp;edition=prelim">review only final judgments or decrees</a> issued by the highest court of a state. The Colorado Supreme Court ruling is not a final judgment on the entire case, so the U.S. Supreme Court could decide that it is too soon to intervene.</p>

<p>Another wrinkle appeared a week before the oral arguments: On Sept. 28, 2026, the court announced that <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/DocketPDF/25/25-170/425819/20260928133032324_Letter%20to%20Counsel%20in%20No.%2025-170.pdf">Justice Samuel Alito would no longer participate</a> in hearings and deliberations in the Suncor case. No reason was given, but Alito has been under pressure to <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/09/justice-alito-will-no-longer-participate-in-climate-change-dispute/">recuse himself based on his financial holdings in several oil companies</a>. His decision raises the prospect of a split 4-4 decision, which would be a victory for Boulder and leave the Colorado Supreme Court decision in place.</p>

<h2>The law of preemption</h2>

<p>In 1947, the Supreme Court ruled that federal laws should not be presumed to override state law, “<a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/331/218/">unless that was the clear and manifest purpose of Congress</a>” when it passed the laws.</p>

<p>But in a 1992 ruling, the Supreme Court declared that “<a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/505/88/">any state law … which interferes with or is contrary to federal law, must yield</a>.” </p>

<p>There are basically two kinds of preemption: express and implied. </p>

<p>An example of express preemption is the Supreme Court’s June 2026 ruling in <a href="https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1068_n7ip.pdf">Monsanto v. Durnell</a> that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act did expressly preempt a state law that required warnings on potentially harmful pesticides. Under that state law, a jury had required chemical giant Monsanto to <a href="https://theconversation.com/supreme-court-bars-states-from-protecting-consumers-if-federal-agencies-wont-284609">pay more than $1 million in compensation</a> to a person who had been harmed by exposure to glyphosate, a pesticide sold under the commercial name Roundup. The Supreme Court found that Congress had intended the federal law to supersede any inconsistent state laws.</p>

<p>Implied preemption is more complicated. A state law can be preempted where it conflicts with a federal law, such as conflicts over <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/570/1/">voter registration</a>, or where it creates an obstacle to accomplishing a federal objective, such as where a state law requiring air bags would frustrate more flexible federal rules on <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/529/861/">passive restraints</a> in cars. A state law can also be superseded by a federal law where Congress has created a comprehensive regulatory regime that totally occupies an area of law, as with <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/567/387/">registration of foreign nationals in the U.S</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762854/original/file-20260929-60-c6k8iz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An industrial area is viewed from the air, showing lights and tubes and pipes and metal buildings." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762854/original/file-20260929-60-c6k8iz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762854/original/file-20260929-60-c6k8iz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762854/original/file-20260929-60-c6k8iz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762854/original/file-20260929-60-c6k8iz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762854/original/file-20260929-60-c6k8iz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762854/original/file-20260929-60-c6k8iz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762854/original/file-20260929-60-c6k8iz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The Clean Air Act regulates pollution from industrial facilities as well as vehicles and other sources.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-an-aerial-view-the-marathon-petroleum-corps-los-angeles-news-photo/2269596917">Justin Sullivan/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Assessing the preemption arguments</h2>

<p>Based on the existing law, the companies have a steep hill to climb. </p>

<p>First, the Clean Air Act has contained a specific provision since 1970 that <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/7416">explicitly says the federal law does not overrule state laws</a> providing additional remedies for air pollution. The Supreme Court in 2011 acknowledged that provision <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/564/410/">left the door open</a> for states and cities to seek compensation for climate change impacts under state law.</p>

<p>Second, there is no conflict between the state law and the Clean Air Act: It is possible for a company to comply with both. The federal law regulates air pollution from sources such as automobiles and power plants. It does not regulate consumer fraud, which is the principal basis for Boulder’s lawsuit.</p>

<p>Third, the Clean Air Act does not occupy the entire field of air pollution regulation. In addition to the provision that it doesn’t overrule state laws, the act also declares that <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/7416">states have the authority to set more stringent pollution control standards</a>.</p>

<p>And fourth, when writing and passing the Clean Air Act, Congress specifically chose to <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/7521">preempt state regulations on emissions from new motor vehicles</a>. But it did not block states from regulating industrial sources such as power plants and oil refineries. The choice to block some, but not all, state regulation is powerful evidence that Congress did not intend that federal law should completely eviscerate state law.</p>

<h2>Constitutional arguments</h2>

<p>The companies have claimed <a href="https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/09/the-courts-coming-climate-change-case-and-the-very-confused-doctrine-of-preemption/">states lack authority</a> to address interstate and international sources of pollution unless Congress specifically authorizes it.</p>

<p>But that claim runs up against the <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-10/">10th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution</a>, which establishes the concept of <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/521/898">dual sovereignty</a>: Powers not expressly delegated to Congress are reserved to the states. The Constitution is clear that states have inherent authority to protect their citizens from corporate malfeasance and don’t need Congress’ permission to exercise that power.</p>

<p>The companies also argue that these lawsuits infringe on the federal government’s <a href="https://www.bracewell.com/resources/future-of-climate-liability-litigation-up-in-the-air-in-suncor/">exclusive authority over foreign affairs</a>.</p>

<p>The Supreme Court has considered this type of preemption in very few cases and recognized it only where a state law was deemed to interfere with a specific foreign policy. For instance, in 2000 the court overturned a Massachusetts law that <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/530/363/">barred state agencies from doing business</a> with the country of Burma. After that law was passed, Congress passed a federal law regulating U.S. trade with Burma, which the court said superseded the state law.</p>

<p>Extending this type of preemption to air pollution would be a dramatic and unlimited expansion of the principle of foreign policy preemption.</p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762850/original/file-20260929-70-qq2kc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two men in suits stand at a lectern." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762850/original/file-20260929-70-qq2kc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762850/original/file-20260929-70-qq2kc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762850/original/file-20260929-70-qq2kc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762850/original/file-20260929-70-qq2kc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762850/original/file-20260929-70-qq2kc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762850/original/file-20260929-70-qq2kc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762850/original/file-20260929-70-qq2kc9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Trump administration undercuts preemption claims</h2>

<p>Since President Donald Trump took office for his second term, the Environmental Protection Agency has <a href="https://www.epa.gov/climate-change/endangerment-and-cause-or-contribute-findings-greenhouse-gases-under-section-202a">shifted the position on climate change</a> that previous administrations had taken. In general, the agency’s current position is that the Clean Air Act does not authorize the federal government to <a href="https://www.epa.gov/regulations-emissions-vehicles-and-engines/final-rule-rescission-greenhouse-gas-endangerment">regulate greenhouse gas emissions</a> at all.  </p>

<p>Those various decisions face court challenges that are still pending. But the Trump administration’s position would nullify the preemption argument: If a federal law can’t and doesn’t regulate greenhouse gas emissions, then it also can’t supersede state laws that seek to do so.</p>

<p>What the Supreme Court will do with this case is hard to predict, but the stakes for climate accountability and corporate liability are massive. A broad ruling in favor of Suncor could <a href="https://climateintegrity.org/lawsuits">effectively kill dozens</a> of similar climate-deception lawsuits filed by cities, counties and states nationwide. That would leave the public on the hook for billions of dollars to cope with the escalating impacts of climate change.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292847/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
