body: People living in Boulder County, Colo., have experienced wildfires, flooding and other climate-related disasters
Jason Connolly/AFP via Getty Images Climate change is causing billions of dollars’ worth of damage every year from floods, fires, droughts and other consequences of a rapidly warming planet
Dozens of states, cities, counties and tribes have sued major oil companies
The lawsuits demand reimbursements for the costs of recovery efforts, reconstruction and work to protect people and property from climate-related damage

The crux of their argument is an allegation of fraud, a claim that the companies knew they were contributing to climate change but did not tell the public the truth about how burning fossil fuels warms the climate

It has been well established that company scientists at Exxon and other fossil fuel companies accurately predicted global temperature increases and warned that sharply curtailing fossil fuels was the only way to avoid severe warming
Rather than alerting the public, however, the companies funded climate-denial front groups and promoted false narratives to delay transitions away from fossil fuels
In general, the companies have responded by saying federal laws and the U.S
Constitution preclude any claims for recovery of the costs taxpayers have borne
Supreme Court will hear arguments on Oct. 5, 2026, in Suncor Energy v
County Commissioners of Boulder County , a case that specifically considers the question of whether federal law prohibits these cost-recovery efforts
The outcome of this decision will have enormous consequences for communities already saddled with funding the massive costs of adapting to a changing climate
Potentially complicating an already complex situation, recent moves by the Trump administration may undercut the companies’ arguments
Boulder, Colo., residents look at flooding damage after heavy rains in 2013

Marc Piscotty/Getty Images The Suncor case In 2018, Boulder County sued Suncor and Exxon in Colorado state court, seeking payment for past and expected future damage it blames on the companies’ fossil fuel businesses
Boulder says it has spent millions of dollars – and expects to spend even more in the future – on measures to protect the community against climate-related disasters such as wildfires and flooding
The companies responded that federal law, specifically the Clean Air Act , prevents them from being held responsible under state law

In 2025, the Colorado Supreme Court rejected the companies’ argument , holding that the lawsuit is a valid legal challenge regarding public deception and local costs, rather than an impermissible attempt to regulate federal emissions
The Colorado Supreme Court sent the case back to the lower court for trial
Protestors have argued for years that fossil fuel companies knew about the climate damage their products were causing
Johnny Silvercloud via Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA The justices agreed to hear arguments about the state Supreme Court’s decision, but there is a potential catch
Supreme Court can review only final judgments or decrees issued by the highest court of a state
The Colorado Supreme Court ruling is not a final judgment on the entire case, so the U.S
Supreme Court could decide that it is too soon to intervene

Another wrinkle appeared a week before the oral arguments: On Sept. 28, 2026, the court announced that Justice Samuel Alito would no longer participate in hearings and deliberations in the Suncor case
No reason was given, but Alito has been under pressure to recuse himself based on his financial holdings in several oil companies
His decision raises the prospect of a split 4-4 decision, which would be a victory for Boulder and leave the Colorado Supreme Court decision in place

The law of preemption In 1947, the Supreme Court ruled that federal laws should not be presumed to override state law, “ unless that was the clear and manifest purpose of Congress ” when it passed the laws

But in a 1992 ruling, the Supreme Court declared that “ any state law … which interferes with or is contrary to federal law, must yield .” There are basically two kinds of preemption: express and implied
An example of express preemption is the Supreme Court’s June 2026 ruling in Monsanto v
Durnell that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act did expressly preempt a state law that required warnings on potentially harmful pesticides

Under that state law, a jury had required chemical giant Monsanto to pay more than $1 million in compensation to a person who had been harmed by exposure to glyphosate, a pesticide sold under the commercial name Roundup
The Supreme Court found that Congress had intended the federal law to supersede any inconsistent state laws

A state law can be preempted where it conflicts with a federal law, such as conflicts over voter registration , or where it creates an obstacle to accomplishing a federal objective, such as where a state law requiring air bags would frustrate more flexible federal rules on passive restraints in cars

A state law can also be superseded by a federal law where Congress has created a comprehensive regulatory regime that totally occupies an area of law, as with registration of foreign nationals in the U.S
The Clean Air Act regulates pollution from industrial facilities as well as vehicles and other sources
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Assessing the preemption arguments Based on the existing law, the companies have a steep hill to climb
First, the Clean Air Act has contained a specific provision since 1970 that explicitly says the federal law does not overrule state laws providing additional remedies for air pollution
The Supreme Court in 2011 acknowledged that provision left the door open for states and cities to seek compensation for climate change impacts under state law
Second, there is no conflict between the state law and the Clean Air Act: It is possible for a company to comply with both

<title>Antarctica’s ice loss is locked in, and extra snowfall won’t save it – that’s bad news for low-lying coastal areas elsewhere</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762576/original/file-20260928-50-m9ewz1.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C49%2C1164%2C776&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A glacier front meets the sea in Antarctica. The ice sheet holds enough water to raise global sea level by about 190 feet (58 meters).</span> <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Qiyue Sun</span></span></figcaption></figure><p>Sea-level rise is one of the most visible signs of climate change, one that is threatening low-lying coastal communities around the world. Today, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10196-1">about 1 billion people</a> live in coastal areas; about 100 million live within 1 meter (3.3 feet) of sea level, highly exposed to coastal flooding.</p>

<p>Over the long term, when it comes to future sea-level rise, one place matters more than any other: Antarctica. </p>

<p>The frozen continent holds enough ice to raise global sea level by <a href="https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/ice-sheets/ice-sheet-quick-facts">about 190 feet (58 meters)</a>. Yet <a href="https://doi.org/10.5194/tc-14-3033-2020">scientists have disagreed</a> on a fundamental question: Will Antarctica gain more ice than it loses this century or lose more ice than it gains?</p>

<p>In a new study published in the scientific journal <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-02102-1">Nature Geoscience</a>, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=LKD_TNwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">we</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ceifbhUAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">looked</a> at hundreds of thousands of potential futures and the impact of each on the ice sheet. </p>

<p>We found that Antarctica’s ice loss this century is locked in – even if the world limits global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), the 2015 international <a href="https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-paris-agreement">Paris climate agreement’s</a> most ambitious goal. </p>

<h2>Why the Antarctic ice sheet is so hard to predict</h2>

<p>The Antarctic ice sheet’s future depends on a chain of events.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg1/resources/climate-change-in-data/">Greenhouse gas emissions</a> from vehicles, coal- and natural gas-fueled power plants and other sources around the world determine how much the ocean and air around Antarctica warms. That warming shapes how ice shelves around the continent’s margins melt, and how quickly the glaciers behind them slide over the bedrock. When those ice shelves thin or collapse, studies show the <a href="https://nsidc.org/learn/parts-cryosphere/ice-shelves/why-ice-shelves-matter">glacier flow speeds up</a>.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/wsSD_vuBz-s?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A European research team explains ways Antarctica is vulnerable to ice loss from the ocean and how models work. TiPACCS.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Each step relies on assumptions that scientists have yet to agree on, such as <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/world-of-change/larsen-b/">how ice shelves collapse</a>. Different assumptions give different answers, and because each step feeds the next, the differences grow – what scientists call cascading uncertainty. As a result, research teams around the world can’t agree on whether Antarctica will gain or lose ice this century.</p>

<p>Snow is part of the puzzle. Warmer air holds more moisture, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10912-x">so as temperatures rise, more snow will likely fall on Antarctica</a>. In some projections, that extra snow outweighs the ice lost to the warming ocean, and the ice sheet actually grows.</p>

<h2>Auditioning possible futures</h2>

<p>A big reason for this persistent disagreement involves the cost of computing. </p>

<p>Each ice-sheet simulation runs with just one set of assumptions for every step in the chain, from how much greenhouse gas we emit to how the ice behaves. One run can keep a supercomputer busy for days, so no team can test every plausible combination.</p>

<p>Our team of data scientists, glaciologists and oceanographers took a shortcut. An international project called the Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison Project, or <a href="https://www.ismip.org/research/ismip6">ISMIP6</a>, has built a large archive of Antarctic simulations showing how the ice responds under different circumstances. We trained a physics-informed machine learning model on that archive to learn how each simulation’s outcome depends on its physical assumptions, such as how easily ice slides over bedrock. The machine learning model does in a fraction of a second what took the original models days, predicting sea-level change with similar accuracy.</p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762601/original/file-20260928-50-v03tk2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762601/original/file-20260928-50-v03tk2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762601/original/file-20260928-50-v03tk2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762601/original/file-20260928-50-v03tk2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762601/original/file-20260928-50-v03tk2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762601/original/file-20260928-50-v03tk2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762601/original/file-20260928-50-v03tk2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762601/original/file-20260928-50-v03tk2.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">NASA’s Grace satellite has tracked ice mass loss over the years.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/31158/#media_group_312023">NASA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>That speed let us run millions of combinations and check hundreds of thousands of possible futures against <a href="https://grace.jpl.nasa.gov/mission/grace/">data from satellites</a> that weigh the ice sheet from space by sensing tiny changes in Earth’s gravity. Only scenarios that were able to match what the satellites have seen since 2002 made the cut. </p>

<p>The scenarios that did make the cut point one direction: Antarctica  will <a href="http://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-02102-1">lose more ice than it gains this century</a>, even if humanity is able to <a href="https://www.unep.org/resources/limiting-overshoot-navigating-exceedance">limit global warming to 1.5 C</a>. </p>

<p>That means Antarctica will <a href="https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-global-sea-level">contribute more to sea-level rise</a> that’s already being driven by melting of the Greenland ice sheet and mountain glaciers and from warming ocean temperatures that cause water to expand.</p>

<h2>What a clearer forecast can do</h2>

<p>The biggest lessons from our study are that greenhouse gas emissions matter and <a href="http://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-026-02102-1">extra snowfall won’t save Antarctica</a>. Every ton of greenhouse gas that humans can avoid releasing today reduces how much ice Antarctica loses this century, and the benefit – slower and less sea-level rise – lasts for hundreds of years.</p>

<p>In a scenario with very high emissions, our results show a potential faster domino effect. A fast-warming ocean thins the ice shelves, weakened shelves break apart, and glacier ice flows into the ocean faster. Each step makes the next one easier. Together, these steps could add up to 10 inches (25 centimeters) of sea-level rise from Antarctica alone by 2100 – <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2024EF005914">enough to permanently flood the homes of more than 10 million people</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762594/original/file-20260928-50-cbttbf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An illustration showing different steps in the ice melt" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762594/original/file-20260928-50-cbttbf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762594/original/file-20260928-50-cbttbf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762594/original/file-20260928-50-cbttbf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762594/original/file-20260928-50-cbttbf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762594/original/file-20260928-50-cbttbf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762594/original/file-20260928-50-cbttbf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762594/original/file-20260928-50-cbttbf.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">What different types of models help scientists understand about ice melt, and how they are connected to help predict the Antarctic ice sheet’s future. On the left, how greenhouse gas emissions change the climate, including sea ice, ocean and atmospheric dynamics, which influence one another and levels of global warming. On the right, what goes into an ice sheet model, including ice shelf melt and collapse and how the ice slides. Every stage adds uncertainty.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Yucheng Lin</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Of more than 20 physical assumptions about Antarctica, three matter most for understanding future sea-level rise: <a href="https://www.asoc.org/learn/melting-ice-shelves/">how ice shelves respond</a> to a warming ocean, <a href="https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/topics/cryosphere/glaciers/glacier-power/how-do-glaciers-move">how ice slides over bedrock</a>, and <a href="https://www.asoc.org/learn/heating-oceans/">how fast the ocean and air around Antarctica warm</a>. Gaining a better understanding of these processes would do the most to sharpen sea-level projections.</p>

<h2>What’s still missing</h2>

<p>Our study is far from the final word. </p>

<p>Some processes are missing from today’s simulations, so our machine learning model can’t learn about them – for example, <a href="https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/glacier-processes/structural-glaciology/">how ice cracks and breaks</a>, and how <a href="https://www.antarcticglaciers.org/glacier-processes/glacial-lakes/subglacial-lakes/">rivers and lakes beneath the ice sheet</a> change over time. Any of these could change our understanding of how quickly Antarctica’s ice reaches the sea and whether coastal communities have enough time to adapt. </p>

<p>What our study does offer is a much faster way to test combinations of assumptions that are too costly to simulate one by one. That provides a clearer basis for the decisions coastal communities around the world are already having to make.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293066/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>As AI political deepfakes go viral, lawmakers struggle to keep up – 2 states’ laws show limits of what they can do</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762583/original/file-20260928-50-ofphxz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=636%2C235%2C2650%2C1767&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A woman views a manipulated video in January 2019 that changes what is said by President Donald Trump and former President Barack Obama, illustrating how deepfake technology can deceive viewers.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/woman-in-washington-dc-views-a-manipulated-video-on-january-news-photo/1090433874?adppopup=true">Robe LeverAFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Imagine watching a political campaign video in which a candidate admits to taking a bribe. You recognize the face and voice. But the confession is entirely fabricated, thanks to artificial intelligence.</p>

<p>Now imagine that your state has passed a law against these <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/does-ai-fight-or-fuel-election-disinformation">AI-generated election deepfakes</a>. Would that mean the video has to be removed from the airwaves?</p>

<p>In its June 2026 report, the National Conference of State Legislatures <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/artificial-intelligence-ai-in-elections-and-campaigns">counted 31 states with election deepfake laws</a>. California and Texas enacted their first election-deepfake laws in 2019, but <a href="https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/artificial-intelligence-ai-in-elections-and-campaigns">most states adopted theirs in 2024 or later</a>. Among the 31 states, 28 required disclosures. The other three – Maryland, Minnesota and Texas – prohibited certain election deepfakes, even if the content carried an AI warning.</p>

<p>In many states, a warning telling viewers the content was generated or manipulated using AI can satisfy a government’s disclosure requirement. The fabricated ad can remain in circulation with that warning. </p>

<p>Louisiana, for example, requires AI warnings on certain campaign ads that falsely depict candidates and campaign calls that use artificial versions of public figures’ voices. Maryland, meanwhile, prohibits certain deceptive election deepfakes even when they carry a warning.</p>

<p>I am <a href="https://daniels.du.edu/directory/stefani-langehennig/">an AI policy scholar</a> at the University of Denver, where we use an <a href="https://du-caid.github.io/tracker/">AI policy tracker</a> to monitor bills and laws across the U.S. With 2026 midterm elections approaching, the important question for voters is what protection a deepfake law actually provides, and I examine two state laws – in Louisiana and Maryland – to illustrate the limits of what can be done.</p>

<h2>When a warning is enough</h2>

<p>Consider a political campaign ad that uses AI to put a candidate’s face onto someone else’s body, making it look as though the candidate said or did something that never happened. </p>

<p><a href="https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1486310">A June 2026 Louisiana law</a> requires a clear warning about AI use in ads that meet these conditions. The rule applies to certain messages urging people to vote for or against a candidate, including printed materials, online advertisements and broadcasts.</p>

<p>As for videos, adding the required warning can satisfy the disclosure requirement in the Louisiana law. The warning tells voters how the content was made, not whether its accusations are true. It also does not excuse violations of other laws.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://petapixel.com/2023/04/25/republicans-launch-entirely-ai-generated-ad-attacking-president-biden/">2023 Republican National Committee ad</a> attacking former President Joe Biden illustrates this distinction. It depicted an imagined future after Biden’s reelection, with a warning: “Built entirely with AI imagery.” Although it predates Louisiana’s law, it shows how a disclosure can accompany an ad without stopping its circulation.</p>

<p>But this protection does not cover every candidate on the ballot. The Louisiana law <a href="https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1486310">excludes candidates for federal office</a>. A fabricated video about a congressional candidate, therefore, does not need an AI warning.</p>

<p>For ads involving state and local candidates, leaving out a required warning can have serious consequences. Violators who are found to damage a candidate’s reputation or deceive voters can face a fine of up to US$2,000, up to two years in prison or both. <a href="https://legis.la.gov/legis/Law.aspx?d=112643">Local district attorneys</a> generally decide whether to prosecute, subject to the state attorney general’s supervision.</p>

<p>Louisiana also requires AI disclosures in certain campaign calls, including robocalls. Under <a href="https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/BillInfo.aspx?i=250501">a May 2026 law</a>, calls that use AI to reproduce a public figure’s voice must disclose that use at the beginning of the call. The state’s board of ethics enforces the requirement. Violators can face civil fines of up to $2,500 for a first violation and $5,000 for subsequent violations.</p>

<h2>When a warning will not do</h2>

<p>Maryland takes a different approach to deceptive election content, prohibiting certain deepfakes even when they carry an AI warning. </p>

<p><a href="https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2026RS/chapters_noln/Ch_444_sb0141E.pdf">Maryland’s May 2026 law</a> covers images, audio and video created or altered with AI or other digital tools to falsely depict a person in a way that looks or sounds genuine. Adding a label to that fabricated confession would not, by itself, make it lawful.</p>

<p>Whether someone violates the law also depends on their actions and purpose. They must knowingly or recklessly create, use or spread a deepfake to produce materially false information, with an intent such as influencing a voting decision. </p>

<p>The law separately requires actual or intended harm to a voter, potential voter or ballot petition, but does not define that harm. Misleading voters about a candidate alone does not automatically establish a violation. A conviction can bring a fine of up to $5,000, up to five years in prison or both.</p>

<p>Maryland also gives election officials <a href="https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2026RS/chapters_noln/Ch_444_sb0141E.pdf">ways to respond</a> when false voting information is spread.</p>

<p>The state’s top election administrator must publicly correct credible reports of misinformation about voting procedures, results or rights. For example, Maryland’s State Board of Elections has a <a href="https://elections.maryland.gov/press_room/rumor_control.html">rumor control page</a> to monitor disinformation. The administrator can seek court-ordered removal of misinformation, though not against online services hosting others’ posts.</p>

<p>These powers do not let election officials remove every false claim about a candidate. <a href="https://mgaleg.maryland.gov/2026RS/fnotes/bil_0001/sb0141.pdf">The public can report election misinformation</a>, and officials can pass those reports to the state attorney general.</p>

<p>Maryland’s reporting system dates to a 2024 law, but its deepfake prohibition and new removal authority took effect June 1, 2026. Neither guarantees that a correction will reach voters before they cast their ballots.</p>

<p>By early September 2026, the Wesleyan Media Project had identified at least <a href="https://mediaproject.wesleyan.edu/releases-090426/">164 political ads nationwide created or enhanced with AI</a> during the 2026 election cycle, accounting for nearly $80 million in ad spending. About 7 in 10 ads carried no AI disclosure, although the count includes uses beyond deceptive impersonations and does not establish how many ads violated a law or misled voters.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762585/original/file-20260928-60-ue1808.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Several images of a man and woman appear on social media feeds." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762585/original/file-20260928-60-ue1808.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762585/original/file-20260928-60-ue1808.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762585/original/file-20260928-60-ue1808.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762585/original/file-20260928-60-ue1808.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762585/original/file-20260928-60-ue1808.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762585/original/file-20260928-60-ue1808.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762585/original/file-20260928-60-ue1808.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In this photo illustration created in May 2026, AI-generated images posted on AI influencers’ social media accounts depict a blonde woman lavishing praise on President Donald Trump while criticizing his rivals.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/this-photo-illustration-created-on-may-7-shows-ai-generated-news-photo/2275322853?adppopup=true">Chris Delmas/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Does a warning change anyone’s mind?</h2>

<p>Warnings can make people more skeptical of misleading content. However, whether that affects what they share or how they vote is a separate question.</p>

<p>A 2025 study <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgaf170">tested warning labels on misleading AI-generated images</a> in two experiments involving 7,579 Americans. People who saw the labels were less likely to believe the posts’ claims. However, warnings that simply identified content as AI-generated did little to change how willing people said they were to engage with it, including sharing it.</p>

<p>Warning labels can also raise doubts about accurate information. Another recent study found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae403">people rated headlines as less accurate</a> when they were labeled as AI-generated, regardless of whether the headlines were true or false. Knowing that AI helped produce something does not tell a reader whether its claims are correct.</p>

<p>Neither study tested whether a state’s disclosure law changes how people vote. The studies also cannot tell us whether the threat of punishment under Maryland’s law discourages people from creating or spreading deepfakes. </p>

<h2>Deepfake enforcement</h2>

<p>Passing a law also does not settle whether officials can enforce it. </p>

<p>In September 2026, a federal judge temporarily barred Montana from <a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/us-judge-blocks-montana-enforcing-deepfake-election-ads-law-against-conservative-2026-09-17/">enforcing its deepfake law</a>, finding that it likely posed a threat to a conservative PAC’s free speech rights under the <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-1/">First Amendment</a>.</p>

<p>For voters, gaps in what disclosure laws cover mean that a video without an AI warning has not necessarily passed an authenticity test. The disclosure rule might not cover it, as with congressional candidates under <a href="https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1486310">Louisiana’s provision</a>.</p>

<p>Moreover, someone may have ignored the law. A warning’s absence cannot tell viewers of the AI content which explanation applies.</p>

<p>So, back to that video of a candidate apparently admitting to taking a bribe. </p>

<p>It could still reach voters under both Louisiana’s and Maryland’s laws. In Louisiana, a video covered by the disclosure rule can circulate with the required warning. In Maryland, creating or spreading it could lead to punishment if the law’s conditions are not met. Neither approach guarantees that voters will avoid seeing the fabricated confession before casting their ballots. </p>

<p>These laws give states ways to respond to deception, but their passage alone cannot guarantee voters that what they are watching is real.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292107/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
<p class="fine-print"><em><span>Stefani Langehennig receives funding from the American Political Science Association&#39;s (APSA) Centennial Center Research Center. </span></em></p></content>

<title>Why the nor'easter’s storm surge was so high, and what it says about the El Niño winter ahead</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762902/original/file-20260929-60-p6owwj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5000%2C3333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A nor&#39;easter&#39;s storm surge swept into restaurants and homes in Sea Bright, N.J., in late September 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/APTOPIX%20NJ%20Extreme%20Weather/1c2e87ae3c2f45e39974bd1c5edeac05/photo">AP Photo/Andres Kudacki</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>As a <a href="https://apnews.com/video/a-powerful-noreaster-pummels-the-shoreline-in-the-eastern-u-s-causing-travel-disruption-abcf6e7b21094627b22b09e1787c3887">powerful nor’easter</a> hit the U.S. Atlantic Coast in late September 2026, the ocean poured into coastal neighborhoods from North Carolina to New York. Water from the storm surge and heavy rain filled streets and surrounded homes as near-hurricane-force winds knocked out power. It may have <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/27/nx-s1-5982785/nantucket-shipwreck-uncovered-by-noreaster">even uncovered a shipwreck more than a century old</a>.</p>

<p>Atlantic City, New Jersey, saw its highest water level since Superstorm Sandy in 2012, as the storm surge <a href="https://whyy.org/articles/noreaster-flooding-new-jersey-2026/">washed into houses and vehicles and eroded protective beach dunes</a>.</p>

<p>I <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=kXsr-UMAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">study storm systems</a>. People may be wondering if the nor’easter flooding is a prelude for what to expect as a <a href="https://theconversation.com/2026s-el-nino-is-shaping-up-to-be-a-doozy-its-already-affecting-global-shipping-fish-behavior-and-heat-291490">strong El Niño</a> continues to build this winter and as sea level rises in the future. To understand the risks, let’s break down what caused the water to rise so high.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="An animation shows swirling wind patterns along the coast." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762884/original/file-20260929-50-c81kez.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762884/original/file-20260929-50-c81kez.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762884/original/file-20260929-50-c81kez.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762884/original/file-20260929-50-c81kez.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762884/original/file-20260929-50-c81kez.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762884/original/file-20260929-50-c81kez.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762884/original/file-20260929-50-c81kez.gif?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A computer model forecasts the nor'easter’s winds in late September 2026, showing how they pushed water onshore.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><span class="source">Brian Tang, NOAA images</span></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The storm surge</h2>

<p>Several factors go into high water levels, and they combined to worsen flooding during the nor’easter.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/surge/">Storm surge</a> is the piling up of water caused by strong winds pushing water onshore. As the nor’easter began to take shape, gale-force winds began pushing water over hundreds of miles of the Atlantic toward the coast. As the storm strengthened and its pressure dropped, the winds grew stronger and this push of water intensified.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762924/original/file-20260929-60-vfi7or.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A tall residential building with a partially collapsed and eroded dune." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762924/original/file-20260929-60-vfi7or.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762924/original/file-20260929-60-vfi7or.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762924/original/file-20260929-60-vfi7or.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762924/original/file-20260929-60-vfi7or.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762924/original/file-20260929-60-vfi7or.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762924/original/file-20260929-60-vfi7or.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762924/original/file-20260929-60-vfi7or.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Fences and sand dunes lie in ruin along Maryland’s Ocean City Beach on Sept. 28, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/fences-and-sand-dunes-lay-in-ruin-along-ocean-city-beach-on-news-photo/2297616261?adppopup=true">Finn Gomez/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>There are four basic factors that determine the surge height at any given location: the strength of the onshore wind, the size of the storm, the shape of the coastline and the depth of the ocean.</p>

<p>The September 2026 surge was highest where the water was directed into shallow bays and inlets. In those areas, the push of water becomes concentrated into a small area with nowhere to go but onto land. Some of the largest surges during the nor’easter were in <a href="https://www.nj.com/weather/2026/09/repeated-flooding-is-what-set-weekend-noreaster-apart-from-sandy-experts-say.html">Raritan Bay in New Jersey</a> and Delaware Bay.</p>

<p>The slow movement of the nor’easter up the East Coast resulted in a large, sustained surge.</p>

<p><iframe id="StqlU" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/StqlU/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Storm surge in Delaware during the nor'easter"></iframe></p>

<h2>High tides raised the flood risk</h2>

<p>Inundation – the actual water level above the ground – depends on both the storm surge and the tide.</p>

<p>The greatest flooding occurs when the peak storm surge coincides with high tide. Worse yet is when the high tides are higher than normal, such as around a full moon. The <a href="https://www.britannica.com/video/How-does-the-Moon-affect-the-tides/-320503">gravitational pull</a> of <a href="https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/tutorial_tides/tides06_variations.html">both the Moon and the Sun</a> combine around a full moon to make the tides larger. That’s what happened during the height of the nor’easter.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762736/original/file-20260929-50-ipnay5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An illustration shows the moon's pull on the ocean" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762736/original/file-20260929-50-ipnay5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762736/original/file-20260929-50-ipnay5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762736/original/file-20260929-50-ipnay5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762736/original/file-20260929-50-ipnay5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762736/original/file-20260929-50-ipnay5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762736/original/file-20260929-50-ipnay5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762736/original/file-20260929-50-ipnay5.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The phenomenon of tides is primarily driven by the Moon’s gravitational influence on the ocean.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.noaa.gov/education/resource-collections/ocean-coasts/tides">NOAA Education</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Additionally, the long duration of the nor’easter allowed inundation to occur over multiple high tides, resulting in repeated rounds of coastal flooding.</p>

<h2>The role of sea-level rise</h2>

<p>Another important factor for inundation is sea-level rise. Sea-level rise is occurring because the planet is warming. That melts glaciers, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-026-08088-0">sending more water into the oceans</a>, and <a href="https://courses.ems.psu.edu/earth107/node/1502">causes the ocean to physically expand</a>.</p>

<p>Sea-level rise is occurring faster in parts of the U.S. East Coast compared with other areas, primarily due to something called <a href="https://www.whoi.edu/press-room/news-release/why-is-sea-level-rising-higher-in-some-places-along-u-s--east-coast-than-others/">post-glacial rebound</a>. The weight of the Laurentide ice sheet that covered large parts of North America thousands of years ago pushed down the land below it, while causing the land around its edges to rise – including along the mid-Atlantic seaboard. As the ice melted, those edges that had lifted slowly sank again.</p>



<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762737/original/file-20260929-50-22tpuh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762737/original/file-20260929-50-22tpuh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762737/original/file-20260929-50-22tpuh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=571&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762737/original/file-20260929-50-22tpuh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=571&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762737/original/file-20260929-50-22tpuh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=571&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762737/original/file-20260929-50-22tpuh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=718&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762737/original/file-20260929-50-22tpuh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=718&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762737/original/file-20260929-50-22tpuh.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=718&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Arrows represent the direction and magnitude of relative sea-level change along the U.S. East Coast.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/trends-and-extremes/main-product.html?mapTab=station&amp;amp;tab=trends&amp;amp;station-id=8534720&amp;amp;plot=relative-sea-level-change-ntde&amp;tab=trends">NOS/NOAA/CO-OPS</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In Atlantic City, <a href="https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/trends-and-extremes/main-product.html?mapTab=station&amp;tab=trends&amp;station-id=8534720&amp;plot=relative-sea-level-change-ntde">sea level is rising</a> at a rate of <a href="https://njclimateresourcecenter.rutgers.edu/resources/nj-sea-level-rise-reports/">about 2 inches (50 millimeters) every decade</a>. A couple of inches can mean the difference between water staying out of one’s house or pouring in. Even if nor’easters don’t become stronger in the future, they will become more damaging because sea level is already higher, and more places will experience flooding.</p>

<h2>More to come this El Niño winter?</h2>

<p>With one of the strongest El Niños in recent memory already <a href="https://theconversation.com/2026s-el-nino-is-shaping-up-to-be-a-doozy-its-already-affecting-global-shipping-fish-behavior-and-heat-291490">affecting weather patterns</a> around the world, is this early-season nor’easter a sign of things to come? It’s difficult to say.</p>

<p>One study found that strong nor’easters along the East Coast are <a href="https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/clim/21/1/2007jcli1705.1.xml">more likely during El Niño years</a>. </p>

<p>Computer model seasonal forecasts suggest an <a href="https://charts.ecmwf.int/products/seasonal_system5_standard_rain?area=NAME&amp;base_time=202609010000&amp;stats=tsum&amp;valid_time=202612020000">increased chance of above-normal precipitation</a> along the East Coast during the winter. This suggests moisture-laden storms with heavy precipitation may be more likely to move up the coast with damaging storm surges.</p>

<p>However, every El Niño is different, and there are few past El Niños close to the strength expected this time to compare with.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762927/original/file-20260929-50-x48njf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762927/original/file-20260929-50-x48njf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762927/original/file-20260929-50-x48njf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762927/original/file-20260929-50-x48njf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762927/original/file-20260929-50-x48njf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762927/original/file-20260929-50-x48njf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762927/original/file-20260929-50-x48njf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762927/original/file-20260929-50-x48njf.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A family carries their belongings through the water of a flooded road during a nor'easter storm on Sept. 26, 2026, in Point Pleasant, N.J., where a voluntary evacuation had been issued.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/family-carries-their-belongings-through-the-water-of-a-news-photo/2296750646?adppopup=true">Ryan Murphy/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The best advice this El Niño winter is to be proactive in preparing and monitoring the weather. Check your insurance policies to understand your coverage, particularly if you are in a flood-prone area. Have an <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-goes-into-a-disaster-kit-and-go-bag-heres-a-checklist-for-wildfires-hurricanes-and-other-storms-168638">emergency supply kit</a> and make sure its contents are refreshed. </p>

<p>Should a big storm threaten, pay attention to the weather forecast from trusted sources and listen to the advice of your community’s emergency managers to keep everyone safe.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293082/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Criminal conspiracy to steal used cooking oil shows how trash can become treasure</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762357/original/file-20260925-50-cxs83l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2400%2C1600&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A restaurant owner looks at a tank for collecting used cooking oil.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/romeo-auer-owner-of-barona-bay-restaurant-and-bar-in-news-photo/1482891987">Steve Pfost/Newsday RM via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Federal prosecutors recently described an interstate criminal enterprise with all the trappings of organized crime: <a href="https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdia/pr/two-new-yorkers-who-are-chinese-nationals-plead-guilty-racketeering-conspiracy">clandestine warehouses, money laundering and stolen goods transported across state lines</a>. The mid-September 2026 announcement stated that 19 defendants faced charges; two had just pleaded guilty, while the remainder are slated for trial in April 2027.</p>

<p>The stolen material was not drugs, guns or jewels. It was leftover cooking oil. </p>

<p>According to prosecutors, members of the group <a href="https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdia/pr/two-new-yorkers-who-are-chinese-nationals-plead-guilty-racketeering-conspiracy">drove trucks to restaurants in 10 states</a>, siphoned used cooking oil from collection tanks and transported it to depots for resale. The alleged motive was simple: Used cooking oil has value. It can be <a href="https://biofuels-news.com/news/the-conversion-of-used-cooking-oils-into-biodiesel/">refined into biodiesel</a>. A viscous fluid that the food industry formerly considered garbage has become valuable enough to spur a large-scale criminal operation.</p>

<p>This oil-theft scheme points to a larger lesson. People tend to think of waste as trash, sewage, slag, manure and other seemingly useless or disgusting substances. But historians, anthropologists and geographers increasingly recognize that <a href="https://discardstudies.com/what-is-discard-studies/">“waste” is a category defined by humans</a>. Technologies, markets, laws and cultural assumptions all determine what is discarded, what is kept and why. Waste describes a material’s status, not necessarily its substance.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.amherst.edu/people/facstaff/emelillo">an environmental historian</a> who studies how societies transform nature into commodities, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=JZ47qkkAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">I</a> am also interested in the other side of the process: how materials classified as waste can be converted back into things of value.</p>

<h2>Making matter into ‘waste’</h2>

<p>Nothing in nature is wasted. A <a href="https://theconversation.com/life-after-death-from-burned-trees-to-bleached-corals-how-dead-organisms-live-on-as-the-building-blocks-of-new-life-283745">fallen tree becomes food for fungi and insects</a>, while its nutrients eventually return to the soil or the atmosphere; animal feces feed creatures ranging from bacteria to dung beetles. In ecosystems, one organism’s leftovers routinely provide for another’s needs.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/737923/original/file-20260525-83-mat2au.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Trees of different ages grow from a fallen log." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/737923/original/file-20260525-83-mat2au.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/737923/original/file-20260525-83-mat2au.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/737923/original/file-20260525-83-mat2au.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/737923/original/file-20260525-83-mat2au.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/737923/original/file-20260525-83-mat2au.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/737923/original/file-20260525-83-mat2au.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/737923/original/file-20260525-83-mat2au.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=501&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A fallen log serves as a nursery for a new hemlock tree in British Columbia, Canada, hence the nicknames nursery log or nurse log.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nursery_Log_at_Schooner_Trail.jpg">Wing-Chi Poon</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Human societies, by contrast, frequently remove unwanted materials from circulation. The question of where those materials go – and whether they remain useless – is part of the history of waste.</p>

<p>Scholars in a growing field called “<a href="https://discardstudies.com/">discard studies</a>” examine this process. Sociologist Zsuzsa Gille describes different “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-954X.12036">waste regimes</a>,” the ideologies and concepts that people use to determine what’s valuable and what’s disposable.</p>

<p>Calling something “waste” does not mean that its physical properties are irrelevant. A toxic chemical can poison a river. But whether people dump, recycle, store or reprocess that substance – and whether they classify it as waste at all – depends on human decisions.</p>

<p>Industrialization did not invent waste, <a href="https://energyhistory.yale.edu/water-power-industrial-manufacturing-and-environmental-transformation-in-19th-century-new-england/">but it dramatically changed its scale and geography</a>. During the 19th century, factories and processing plants brought raw materials together in unprecedented quantities and consolidated their unwanted residues in the same sites. That concentration created disposal problems. It also generated new incentives to find profitable uses for what industry left behind.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762359/original/file-20260925-50-62v3cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An overhead view shows people separating milk curds from whey liquid." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762359/original/file-20260925-50-62v3cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/762359/original/file-20260925-50-62v3cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762359/original/file-20260925-50-62v3cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762359/original/file-20260925-50-62v3cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762359/original/file-20260925-50-62v3cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762359/original/file-20260925-50-62v3cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/762359/original/file-20260925-50-62v3cj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Making cheese involves separating curds from whey.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/helen-feete-co-owner-and-ana-arguello-cheese-maker-process-news-photo/1244715737">Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Manufacturing a demand</h2>

<p>Consider whey. Cheesemaking produces extraordinary quantities of the watery liquid left behind after milk coagulates. For much of the 19th and 20th centuries, <a href="https://doi.org/10.17113/ftb.59.02.21.6968">cheese manufacturers disposed of the whey as an unwanted residue</a>. Dumped into waterways, whey encourages bacterial and algal growth that depletes oxygen and can damage aquatic ecosystems.</p>

<p>Beginning in the 1970s, ultrafiltration allowed producers to <a href="https://doi.org/10.3168/jds.S0022-0302(71)86039-3">separate and concentrate whey proteins</a>. A troublesome liquid became whey powder, lactose and protein concentrates, all of which can be used in baked goods, infant formula, animal feed and protein supplements.</p>

<p>Coal-fired power plants provide another example. Coal combustion leaves behind <a href="https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/pavement/recycling/fach01.cfm">fly ash</a>, a fine mineral residue that companies dumped in landfills or stored in enormous ash ponds. In the 1930s, engineers discovered that fly ash could replace a portion of the Portland cement normally used to <a href="https://www.engr.psu.edu/ce/courses/ce584/concrete/library/materials/Altmaterials/Altmaterialsmain.htm">make concrete</a>. This new application diverted waste from disposal while reducing demand for energy-intensive cement production.</p>

<p>There is much to admire in these transformations. Repurposing leftover materials can reduce pollution, conserve resources and lower the amount of material dumped into landfills or waterways. The ecological ideal of “<a href="https://sustainabilityguide.eu/methods/cradle-to-cradle/">cradle-to-cradle</a>” design rests on precisely this insight. Just as in nature, the output of one process can become the input of another.</p>

<h2>When recycling creates new problems</h2>

<p>Yet finding a market for waste does not necessarily solve the problems that the waste created in the first place.</p>

<p>Cottonseed provides a striking example. During the 19th century, American cotton growers regarded seeds as <a href="https://www.ncpedia.org/cottonseed">an enormous nuisance</a>. Cotton ginning generated mountains of seeds, and many operators simply dumped these unwanted byproducts into nearby waterways, where they accumulated in foul-smelling, decaying masses. The problem became serious enough that Southern states began <a href="https://www.westonaprice.org/health-topics/cotton-seed-toxicity/">restricting cottonseed dumping</a> in the mid-1800s.</p>

<p>Then manufacturers learned to crush cottonseed for oil to be used in soap, cooking and as a substitute for animal fats. They turned the remaining material into fertilizer and animal feed. By the late 19th century, something previously seen as garbage had become the foundation of a major new industry.</p>

<p>Cottonseed boosters proclaimed a transformation of waste into wealth. In 1911, entrepreneur Luther A. Ransom celebrated cottonseed’s ability to produce “<a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/su9040579">edible oil without olives</a>; medicinal oil without codfish; butter without cows; ice cream without cream; lard without hogs.”</p>

<p>But manufacturers also <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/foods12010199">sometimes diluted more expensive olive oil and lard with cheap cottonseed oil</a>. Beginning in the early 20th century, the <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/chemistry/hydrogenation/">chemical process of hydrogenation</a> allowed producers to turn liquid vegetable oils into semisolid fats suitable for shortening and margarine. Partial hydrogenation also produced <a href="https://medlineplus.gov/ency/patientinstructions/000786.htm">artificial trans fats</a>, which were eventually linked to increased cardiovascular risk.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.npr.org/sections/thesalt/2012/01/09/144918710/the-forgotten-fascinating-saga-of-crisco">In 1911, Procter &amp; Gamble introduced Crisco</a>, a vegetable shortening made from hydrogenated cottonseed oil. Consumers could use Crisco in place of lard or butter for frying and baking. Decades before the <a href="https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/fats-and-cholesterol/types-of-fat/transfats/">heart disease risks</a> of <a href="https://www.fda.gov/food/food-additives-petitions/final-determination-regarding-partially-hydrogenated-oils-removing-trans-fat">partially hydrogenated oils</a> were understood, the company <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/how-crisco-made-americans-believers-industrial-food-180973845/">marketed Crisco as an expression of purity</a> and modern food technology.</p>

<p>The problem was not that cottonseed oil was secretly “waste.” It was that industrial processing widened the gap between what manufacturers knew about a product’s origins and composition and what consumers understood about those attributes. Turning a discarded material into a valuable commodity solved one problem while creating another. Consumers increasingly had to trust manufacturers to tell them what they were buying.</p>

<p>Sewage sludge presents an even sharper dilemma. Wastewater treatment produces nutrient-rich dregs that can be processed into biosolids and spread on farmland, <a href="https://www.cambi.com/blog/biosolids-fertilizer">returning nitrogen and phosphorus to soils</a>. But wastewater also carries contaminants. Researchers have found <a href="https://www.epa.gov/pfas/pfas-explained">a group of chemicals known as PFAS</a> – persistent and potentially harmful “forever chemicals” more formally known as perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances – in some sewage sludge. Their presence raises concerns that a system designed to salvage nutrients can also recycle pollutants.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The value of being ‘waste’</h2>

<p>Used cooking oil seems like an almost perfect example of recycling. Refiners turn oil discarded by restaurants and other waste fats into transportation fuel, extracting additional value from crops already grown and oils that have already served their original purpose.</p>

<p>But government policies regarding clean fuel have made some products that carry the label “waste” economically valuable. Because fuels made from <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/us-epa-says-it-is-auditing-biofuel-producers-used-cooking-oil-supply-2024-08-07/">used cooking oil can qualify for financial incentives</a> unavailable to some virgin oils, demand has occasionally pushed prices for used oils above those of newly produced vegetable oils. </p>

<p>That creates an unusual temptation: mix cheaper virgin oil into used cooking oil – or simply <a href="https://giannini.ucop.edu/publications/are-update/issues/2024/28/2/controversies-surrounding-us-imports-of-used-cooki/">pass virgin oil off as waste</a>. Researchers and regulators have raised concerns about fraud in the rapidly growing international markets for used cooking oil.</p>

<p>Generating new uses for discarded matter does not eliminate the politics of waste. It can intensify them. Who decides whether something counts as waste? Who profits when something once considered disposable becomes a valuable commodity? And who can verify what a supposedly recycled material actually contains?</p>

<p>Stolen restaurant cooking oil offers an unexpectedly useful way to think about this problem. The fats and oils inside the tank did not physically change when thieves began siphoning them out. What changed was their status and their value.</p>

<p>That transformation captures one of the paradoxes at the heart of the history of waste. Matter is never worthless, but assigning it a price does not necessarily make its environmental and social costs disappear.</p>

<p>Sometimes finding a use for waste solves a disposal problem. Sometimes it merely gives the problem a new price.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292653/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Waste describes a material’s status, not necessarily its substance

Making matter into ‘waste’ Nothing in nature is wasted
A fallen tree becomes food for fungi and insects , while its nutrients eventually return to the soil or the atmosphere; animal feces feed creatures ranging from bacteria to dung beetles

Calling something “waste” does not mean that its physical properties are irrelevant

Industrialization did not invent waste, but it dramatically changed its scale and geography

title: What Democrats are still getting wrong about voters
excerpt: Congressional Democrats outside the US Capitol on May 21, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images With the 2026 midterm elections fast approaching, po
body: Congressional Democrats outside the US Capitol on May 21, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images With the 2026 midterm elections fast approaching, polling increasingly suggests that the GOP is in for a bad time

As the Iran war drives up inflation and fuel prices , Republicans are on the back foot not just in swing states like Michigan, but in redder parts of the map: Iowa, Texas, and maybe even Kansas , among others. (Not to mention Georgia and North Carolina .)  It’s shaping up to be a Democratic wave, in other words, and a major repudiation of President Donald Trump

According to Sarah Longwell, the publisher of political news site the Bulwark, there’s a clear reason why this is the cycle that things seem to be falling apart for Trump, who has dodged scandals and bad poll numbers before. “The average person is often voting on instinctual things,” she explains, “and those instincts are a lot of your animalistic desires for things to be okay materially.” And for many voters right now, things are not okay materially

Longwell would know: She regularly speaks with voters for her podcast, The Focus Group , and she’s the author of the new book How to Eat an Elephant: One Voter at a Time .  Longwell talked with Vox’s Astead Herndon for a special live recording of the America, Actually podcast at the Texas Tribune Festival earlier this month about why voters are both more and less complicated than punditry sometimes suggests, what the future holds for the Republican Party post-Trump, and the lesson Democrats need to learn to capitalize on their wins
Below is an excerpt of Astead’s conversation with Longwell, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
One of the themes in the book is to talk to voters like real adults
What does that mean?  There was a long period of time in our history where the artifice of politics was part of the performance of politics
Those are not the rules of politics in this communications environment anymore
Every single one of you, if you’re a Bulwark person, you interact with me
I am in your ear, and we’re having a conversation
I walked in here and met a bunch of people, and they were like, “I feel like I know you.” And people want to feel like that about their political leaders now
And so they want to know what makes you tick
Are you a real person? And so the artifice of a debate on CNN is starting to feel really stupid, no offense to CNN
And a lot of it is just that artifice is falling away for voters
Donald Trump understood that as a person who had been in people’s living rooms as a performer

Democratic politicians still have not figured it out.  One of the things that comes through in both the book and I think the work that we both do is how voters don’t always fit into those neat ideological boxes

I always tell the story about when I was at the Iowa caucuses, and I remember in 2019 in the Democratic primary, someone telling me they were stuck between Bernie [Sanders] and [former New York City Mayor Michael] Bloomberg, and asking, “How did you get there?” And what was the answer?  I think the short answer was they liked a strong guy where they knew what he believed in
And they did not care which side of that coin that was, as long as it felt consistent and something they could put their hands around
If ideology is not the controlling paradigm for voters, how should we think about the different ways people are sorting themselves right now?  My answer is genuinely not to sort them as much

This is the reason people say things like, “It’s the economy, stupid,” and then everybody gets bored with that answer, and they want to talk about 10 other things because they’re like, “Well, that’s so straightforward.” But I try in the book to say it really is about improving people’s material well-being and ensuring their safety
So you go back to: What are the most human things that people want? They want to be able to afford gas
They want a job [where] they think that they can go up the ladder
They want their kids to get a good education
They want to know that they’re safe in their community
They want to know they’re safe in the places that they go

And Donald Trump and Republicans really do understand: People vote with weird animal instincts.  Now, I bet a lot of the people in this room are college-educated suburban voters, but the average voter in a general election is a 55-year-old white guy without a college degree

The average person is often voting on instinctual things, and those instincts are a lot of your animalistic desires for things to be okay materially — your cost of health care, and then for you to be safe

And so if you think about those base-level desires and then think about what Democrats spend most of their time talking about, you’re like, “Is that the thing that captures all these people?” When I watch Democrats as somebody who’s an immigrant into the Democratic ecosystem, there’s a lot of, like, “And you get a policy, and you get a policy, and you get a policy.” And I don’t really understand that because everybody needs cheaper gas
Everybody needs groceries that they can afford

And so talking about the things that unite us or that everybody needs, to me, is the secret sauce for how Democrats should think about policy.  Three years ago, Democrats thought that being against January 6th was a thing that united everybody
There was a belief that pro-democracy arguments were going to unite people across ideology
Why did that fail in 2024?  I’ve been thinking about this a lot as Trump gets terrible poll after terrible poll, and this is my point
The coup, all of the horrible things he said about women, all of the lawsuits — I mean, he told everybody an election was stolen
Why is he underwater right now? Because of gas prices, because of a war in Iran, because the negative personal consequences of his policies are hitting people

I’m so aware of the frustration where people are like, “Why are people so selfish? Why don’t they think about the bigger picture of democracy?” And one of the things I try not to do is magic words — consultant stuff, because a lot of consultants do that
They’re like, “Say freedom,” and “Say affordability.” There’s nothing to back it up
But the one magic word I do think that Democrats should start using is “America,” and swap it in for “democracy.” And the reason is, voters practice democracy in America by its individual things
So they like the elements of democracy, but they don’t think about them up here as democracy
And also the word democracy now is very polarized, right? Republicans think that Democrats are a threat to democracy because they stole the 2020 election

title: America leaves Iraq, again
excerpt: Iraqis gather in Baghdad to celebrate the withdrawal of US and international coalition forces on September 30, 2026. | Murtadha Al-Sudani/Anadolu via Getty Imag
body: Iraqis gather in Baghdad to celebrate the withdrawal of US and international coalition forces on September 30, 2026. | Murtadha Al-Sudani/Anadolu via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
The last US troops in Iraq formally withdrew today , 23 years after the United States first invaded Iraq and 12 years after it returned to take on the Islamic State

It’s a historic occasion, by many accounts — but also a pretty low-key one: The US has steadily scaled back its presence in Iraq for years as part of a phased drawdown inked by the Biden administration.  That drawdown represents the end of a long (and  often, ugly ) chapter in US military history
The US and its allies deployed tens of thousands of troops to Iraq as part of the larger war on terror that started in 2003.  Those troops left Iraq in 2011

But a smaller contingent returned three years later to stamp out the Islamic State, a violent jihadist group that had gained a major foothold after Western forces left the country.  Neither campaign was particularly popular with the American public in the end, and more than 4,500 Americans have died in Iraq in the past 20 years

Large numbers of civilian casualties, as well as drone strikes that were seen as violations of Iraq’s sovereignty, have also fueled periodic Iraqi protests against American intervention.  As the US withdraws, however, it’s leaving behind some very loose ends
Loose ends that, as we’ll see in a minute, ultimately benefit…Iran
Go a little deeper View Link Don’t quite believe me? Just look at how Iran’s allies are celebrating today’s news

The commander of one Iranian-backed militia in Iraq called the withdrawal “a crushing defeat for the American project.” Both Iran and the United States have spent the past 23 years attempting to shape the new Iraq

Historically, Iran and Iraq were bitter rivals — an enmity probably best demonstrated by Saddam Hussein’s 1980 invasion of Iran.  After the US toppled Hussein in 2003, however, Tehran redoubled its efforts to build political and military clout in the new Iraqi state
It strengthened ties with figures like Hadi al-Amiri, whose Iran-backed Badr Organization has become a major force in Iraqi politics
It poured hundreds of millions of dollars into soft-power projects, like expanding Shiite pilgrimage sites in Iraq
And it funded, equipped, and trained a number of powerful paramilitary groups
Some analysts have warned that the final withdrawal of US troops could embolden Iranian-linked groups in Iraq

That also seems to be a concern on the ground, where ordinary Iraqis have told reporters they fear their country “ could be swallowed up ” by groups linked to Iran.   Already, the Iraqi government has pushed back the deadline for Iranian-backed militia groups to disarm
It was originally supposed to happen on the official date of the US withdrawal — today
It’s an inglorious ending, all told — and a sobering lesson on the limits of American power
The US may have the resources to handily win any military spat it gets itself into
But securing a desired political outcome is a different and more time-consuming project altogether
It doesn’t help that US rivals like Iran seem very willing to play the long game

By dipping in and out of places like Iraq, the US may risk giving Tehran more openings.  One link for later ➨ Don’t throw out that old receipt! It — along with the political mailers, ticket stubs, business cards, product packaging, and other printed ephemera you encounter in your day — is perfectly suited to the newly viral hobby of junk journaling
It can be a powerful creative practice and the ideal antidote to doomscrolling
